utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-95-16-T, the Prosecutor against Zoran Kupreskic, Mirjan Kupreskic, Vlatko Kupreskic, Drago Josipovic, Dragan Papic, Vladimir Santic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Good morning. May I have the appearances, please, for the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Your microphone, Mr. President, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I've got to get used to all this new equipment. Sorry. Appearances for the Prosecution, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Good morning, dear Judges. My name is Franck Terrier, I shall speak French, and I am appearing on behalf of the Prosecution together with Mr. Moskowitz who will speak English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. For the Defence?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Ranko Radovic, attorney from Zagreb, appearing on behalf of Zoran Kupreskic, and I will speak Croatian.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, I am Jadranka Slokovic-Glumac, attorney from Zagreb, appearing on behalf of Mirjan and Zoran Kupreskic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: Your Honours, my name is Borislav Krajina, attorney from Sarajevo, appearing on behalf of Mr. Vlatko Kupreskic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, my name is Zelimir Par, attorney from Zagreb, appearing on behalf of the accused Vlatko Kupreskic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Good morning, I am Luko Susak, appearing on behalf of Mr. Drago Josipovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. I am attorney Petar Pavkovic, defence council for Vladimir Santic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. I am attorney Petar Puliselic, attorney from Zagreb, appearing on behalf of the accused Dragan Papic. On my right, my assistant, Nika Grospic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I hope that all the accused can hear me in a language that is accessible to them. Can you hear me? Now, first of all, I would like to apologise for being late, for the late beginning of our hearing. It's not our fault, but I will ask now the registrar to ask the Dutch police to try to be on time in bringing here all the accused so that every morning we can start at 9.30 sharp. I would like now, first of all, to go through a few outstanding procedural matters. Afterwards, we will hear arguments on some of these matters, and then we intend to break for 30 or 40 minutes to decide on those questions, if any, and before we start the trial proper, we will then go through a few sort of legal housekeeping matters which must be dealt with before we start with the trial proper. Now, let me list what I regard, after reading all these documents, as outstanding matters to be disposed of before we start with our trial. I will list four items, and I will then ask both parties to tell me whether they feel that there are other items which I have probably neglected. The first item which I think we have to discuss is whether or not any brief has been filed by Defence to respond to the Prosecutor's pre-trial brief pursuant to an order signed by Judge Mumba on the 11th of August, so this morning we have received only a document from Mrs. Glumac. I wonder whether the other Defence counsel have also filed any documents. Remember the deadline was last Friday at 1.00 p.m. This is will be the first item. The second item is the motion filed by counsel for Zoran and Mirjan Kupreskic on the 13th of August, and relating to the production of witness statements by the Prosecution. Third item is the consideration of some of the outstanding issues raised in the motion by counsel for Vlatko Kupreskic. This was the motion requesting the withdrawal of indictment. You may remember that Judge Mumba issued an order on this motion dismissing the motion but reserving for this morning any outstanding matters. The last, fourth and last item, is the possible consideration in ex parte proceedings of two ex parte motions filed by the Prosecution. I will ask the Prosecution whether they want to present oral argument on both motions, or on one of them. Of course, this will be ex parte proceedings. After that, we will be ruling. So on all these issues, as I say, we intend to hear -- on most of them to hear arguments from the parties, and then, in our recess this morning, to decide on the matter. After that, we will then resume our deliberations, our hearing, and after dealing with the housekeeping matters, we will then move on to our trial proper, we will commence our trial proper. Now, may I ask the parties whether they feel that there are other matters which I have probably neglected or forgotten to mention here which, in their view, should be dealt with at the outset, before we start with the trial proper? Let me, first of all, turn to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Your Honour, regarding the legal points and issues you mentioned, I can't think of any other issues to deal with. As to housekeeping matters, it may be too soon, too early, to mention them, but I think it might be useful to mention the issue of protective measures to be attributed to some witnesses, and also we should speak about the way the Court believes we should deal with these issues in order to waste as little time as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: May I ask the Defence counsel whether they feel there are other matters which should be discussed? No matters? Yes, please. I apologise, but since we still can't remember your name, could you, when you take the floor, first of all mention your name so that -- gradually in a few days we will of course remember very well all your names.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: Attorney Borislav Krajina appearing on behalf of Borislav Kupreskic. We would say, first of all, that we agree with what you have said, Your Honour, Mr. President, but within the framework of the points you have mentioned, referring to the motion of the Defence of Vlatko Kupreskic, that we also examine and finally deal with the problem of the restoration of the property and documents of the accused Kupreskic, a matter that we have still not managed to resolve, and the Defence considers this to be important. Secondly, we would like our motion and requests for specialist examinations of the accused Kupreskic to be carried out because he's 100 per cent invalid and he has a heart problem as well, a heart condition.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Yes, we will add these two points to our list of outstanding matters. I will therefore start with the first question; namely, whether the other Defence counsel other than Mrs. Glumac intend to file any response to the Prosecutor's pre-trial brief. We have, in reading Mrs. Glumac's brief, we have seen that, according to her, it is too early now for the Defence counsel to file a detailed brief setting out the various points they admit and the points they challenge. I wonder whether the other Defence counsel agree with Mrs. Glumac, and in this case, we would wait for two or three weeks because this is what Mrs. Glumac suggested, that probably, in a few weeks' time, Defence counsel would be in a better position to file detailed briefs. Do all counsel agree with the position taken by Mrs. Glumac? In this case we would later on rule on this matter, but I for one think it is quite appropriate for all of them to get some more time. Yes, Mr. Krajina? Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: I should like to repeat, Your Honour, that we did, in due time, that is seven days after we received the pre-trial brief of the Prosecution, that we did file a reply and respond in detail to that brief.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Mr. President, may I just say that this letter does not have the value of a pre-trial brief. It is just a letter addressed by the Defence team. My intention was to write this on behalf of all because we are all in the same position, and I believe that we would all benefit from some additional time, especially with respect to the legal issues raised in the pre-trial brief of the Prosecution. As for the facts of the matter, may I add a point which is common to all the Defence attorneys? There are some facts that we agree with; therefore, we admit certain facts. But they have been interpreted in such a way and placed in such a context that if we were to elaborate on all the circumstances which, in our view, the Prosecutor has misinterpreted, that would already be a defence proper. So that if we were to start to do this, we would have to comment on each individual point, and this would, in effect, constitute our whole defence, and that is why I think we need to clear up how much of this the Trial Chamber expects us to do in assisting you before the actual trial. So that is our question. To what extent can we enter into some of those counts, because I think the burden of proof is on the Prosecution, and they are the ones that have to present the evidence, and we feel at a disadvantage because we still haven't received all the documents and all the statements, and we already have to start with our defence, so I would like to ask for your assistance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Before I give the floor to other Defence counsel, let me point out that we had in mind, of course, the possibility of the Defence counsel and the Prosecution to come to some sort of agreement on points of fact and law on which they would agree, as we did in Dokmanovic. You may remember in Dokmanovic, after a few weeks, probably three or four weeks, the Prosecution and the Defence were able to come together and prepare a list of facts, not allegations, about the accused, because I realise from your documents that, of course, you contest whatever the Prosecution has stated with regard to all of the accused. But we thought of issues such as whether or not an armed conflict was underway on that particular day, what sort of armed conflict, and other legal issues on legal matters. So I wonder whether, at some stage, you could come together and try to reach a sort of agreement so that we don't need to go into those particular items at great depth. Of course, it depends on you. We don't want to press you. This is only a means of speeding up -- we thought this could be a good way of speeding up the whole trial so that we would concentrate on the major bones of contention on the issues of fact and law and we would, in a way, disregard those particular matters on which both parties fully agree. Let us see whether, in a few weeks' time, you are in a position, after maybe talking with the Prosecution, to come to this sort of agreement, and then you could put on paper, on a document, the various items which are not in dispute between the two parties. Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: My name is Ranko Radovic. In principle, we have nothing against meeting with the Prosecutor, but I think it will be very difficult for us to come to any kind of legal or factual agreement. The only agreement between us and the Prosecution can be over the fact that there was a conflict on the 16th of April in Ahmici. Everything else will be contested. Furthermore, as far as legal issues are concerned, again we have a completely opposite position to the Prosecution. The Prosecution, in its pre-trial brief, refers to precedents from the Tadic case. However, the Tadic case cannot be a precedent for this case since the Tadic case applies to a system of camps or prisons, whereas this case refers to a completely different factual situation. Furthermore, the Prosecutor refers to certain points from the Nuremberg trials, but he forgets that at that trial the leaders of the Nazi system were on trial, whereas in this case persons from the area of Vitez were on trial who were, in fact, defending their homes. In Nuremberg, it was the leaders who were on trial, and here we have people who are at the tail end of events who are on trial, so there is nothing in common between the two. When the time comes, we will elaborate on this point in legal terms but I think the precedents referred to by the Prosecutor cannot be acceptable to us under any conditions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes. Let me again -- thank you so much for your comments. Now, I see that two more Defence counsel would like to address this particular issue. Let me make an appeal to you to be as short as possible because, of course, you may remember that at the outset, when we presented to both parties our guidelines, to which I will come back later on, guidelines for the conduct of proceedings, we insisted that Defence counsel should try not to repeat statements that normally there should be a coordinating Defence counsel who would address issues on behalf of all Defence counsel so as to shorten the time devoted to discussion of particular procedural matters. For the time being, I think it is quite proper for the two Defence counsel to address the particular issue. Yes? Who was first?

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: My name is Petar Puliselic. I should like to be very brief, but I would inform the Court that I too have submitted a separate motion in addition to the joint one by Mrs. Glumac. I have submitted a separate motion in which I refer briefly to the Prosecutor's pre-trial brief. That's all I wanted to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Puliselic. It's a bit difficult, I apologise, but gradually I will learn to pronounce your name.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: My name is Petar Pavkovic appearing on behalf of Vladimir Santic. There is no doubt, Mr. President, the points that you have put on the agenda now merit our special attention, but may I be allowed to refer to the obligation of the Defence so as to avoid the impression that I have now that the Defence has omitted to do something in due course. According to the ruling of the Court on the 28th of July, it had to submit a joint reply to the pre-trial brief and to the indictment. I and my colleagues have fulfilled our obligation and have supplied our responses in relation to the indictment in which we present our positions, so the only thing that remains undisputed between us is that this fact occurred. Everything else is disputed in the position of the Defence. As for our reply to the pre-trial brief of the Prosecution, that brief was received by us very late. Because of the Prosecutor, who did try to explain the delay, but that is the reason why we were unable to meet our obligation in this particular case. Therefore, I agree that we should today establish certain procedural matters so that the Defence may be able to assist the Trial Chamber in understanding its position regarding the indictment. As regards legal matters, I think that we first have to clear up the fact that from Roman times, we know that when we know the facts, only then can we talk about the law. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. To wind up the discussion of this matter, I would say that it is right, as quite a few -- I mean, all Defence counsel have pointed out that -- all of them had already submitted a short response to the request made by the Trial Chamber that they should try to address the points raised in the Prosecution's pre-trial brief. However, since we felt -- and this was also the views of the Prosecution -- that those responses were a bit too concise, we, Judge Mumba, on behalf of the Trial Chamber, in order requested Defence counsel to, and I read out the order, relevant part: "To set out those points, if any, of the indictment in brief which are admitted, those which are denied, and the grounds for so doing and setting out in general terms, setting out in general terms the defence to the indictment." We do appreciate that it is probably too early for the Defence to comply with the order issued by the Trial Chamber, and we hope that, in due time, maybe three, four weeks' time, all Defence counsel, or at least some of them, will be able to produce such documents. It is not a binding request. If you feel that you are not able, as I say, to set out in detail all the points of fact and law which you agree on and those which you contest, so much the better. If you feel that you are not in a position to do so, then we will have to wait until maybe the end of the Prosecution case. By the same token, I would also appeal to you to try see whether you can come to some sort of understanding or agreement with the Prosecution on points of agreement and disagreement. This is again a sort of appeal. Again, if you -- and, of course, you have already understood the rationale behind this appeal from the Court, namely, to try to narrow down the main issues of disagreement. If we are not in a position to do so, we will wait and see what happens later on. I think we should now move on to our next item which is more complex and more serious, but before doing so, I see that Mr. Terrier would like to take the floor. I saw that -- did you intend to address the Court on this particular point?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, if you allow me to, just two brief remarks. Needless to say, the Prosecution sees no problem in granting an additional time for the Defence to submit to the Public Prosecutor and to the Court their respective briefs. I just point out that by doing so, the whole operation becomes less relevant. Indeed, if the facts advanced by the accusation had been admitted by the Defence during the Prosecution case, we would have been in a position to change the way in which the witnesses will appear in order to avoid wasting time. Still, in three weeks' time, such briefs may be of interest, but I do regret this additional delay. The second observation. Of course, I apprise myself of all the briefs that were filed so far, and I have the feeling it may be wrong, but I have the feeling that the Defence counsel in the main have already their own views and positions as to what they admit in the pre-trial brief and what they reject. I mentioned the brief that was filed on behalf of all the Defence counsel. In that brief, whilst there is a request for additional time, it is also mentioned that the only fact admitted by the Defence, is the fact that Bosnia and Herzegovina had proclaimed its independence on the 3rd of March, 1992, and it was recognised as an independent State. As to all the allegations, whether of fact or of law, included in the Prosecution's pre-trial brief seem to be squarely denied or rejected, so even if this delay is granted, I do not think that it would be very useful for the further trial proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Prosecutor. I had another reading of the brief filed by Mrs. Glumac. If I am not wrong, she states towards the end of her brief that the Defence admits the fact that there was an armed conflict on the 16th of April, 1993, so there is another element that is agreed by the Defence. The Defence admits the fact of independence of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina but also admit that there was an armed conflict. This is, of course, one of the main issues raised in this trial. But it admits that there was a conflict, an armed conflict, on the 16th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour, but I note that the concept of armed conflict is a legal issue, a legal concept, but also a military fact or a fact, and as to the facts, the Prosecution does not believe that on the 16th of April, 1993, there was a conflict between two military units or two military camps. This is not a fact that we agree to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: May I suggest then we move on to our next issue; namely, the -- all the questions raised by Mrs. Glumac in her motion filed on the 13th of August, and on this particular matter, I would like -- I apologise for mispronouncing your name. On this issue, I suggest that you, Mrs. Glumac, should briefly comment on the main points of your motion, and then we will ask the Prosecution to respond so that we can hear oral arguments on this particular problem which, as I say, is of crucial importance, and after that we will, in our recess, try to make a ruling on this matter. Please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Your Honours, this motion was submitted for the reason that we feel that the Prosecution did not abide by the provisions of Rule 66 of the Rules of Procedure. Namely, according to those Rules, the Prosecutor was obliged to submit all the witness statements of the witnesses he intends to call, within a time limit of 60 days prior to the beginning of trial. This has not happened. We admit that the first batch came with a four-day delay, and that was acceptable because it was agreed on, but all the statements that reached us later, and they reached us successfully, they kept coming until the 12th of August when the last two statements reached us, and one of them was a statement of a protected witness. That is all right. But before that, a couple of days earlier, the statements of several additional witnesses arrived. Also, there was a whole batch -- I apologise. There was a batch of witness statements that the Defence received around the 21st of July this year which means that this was already late, it was a month late, actually. May I also add that as far as I am aware, the statements of ten witnesses appearing on the Prosecutor's list have not been disclosed, have not been produced. So that we still do not have the complete documents, and we feel that the Defence's right to prepare their defence has thereby been impaired, because we kept receiving these statements one after another. That is why we would appeal to the Court to rule that all those witnesses whose statements reached us after the 60-day time limit, and are not witnesses who enjoy protection granted by the Court, that they should not be called before 60 days has passed from the day when their statements reached us. In this way, our rights would be protected, the Defence would have time to prepare its defence, and I think we would be sanctioning this omission. I know that the material is extensive and that the Prosecution has difficulties, but precisely for those reasons, it has been difficult for the Defence to study those materials and to prepare properly. Rule 67 guarantees the right to a fair trial, and that includes the right to have sufficient time to prepare the Defence case, and we would like to ask, in view of this behaviour by the Prosecutor with regard to the disclosure of documents, that the Court rule along these lines so as to sanction such behaviour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. If I understood you correctly, so you have slightly modified the request you put in your motion because, in your motion, you asked that an order be issued forbidding the Prosecutor to call any witness whose statement has not been made available to the Defence for at least 60 days before the witness is scheduled to testify. I understand now you are requesting that witnesses may be called; however, they should not be called right away or next week, or this week or next week, but only 60 days after their statements have been disclosed to the Defence. Am I correct or did I misunderstand your ...

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: I think you misunderstood, Your Honour. Perhaps it was my problem with my English. I was trying to say that the Prosecutor should not be allowed to call a witness whose statement was not submitted to the Defence 60 days ahead of time; that is, that there should be a 60-day period between the time the statement is disclosed and the appearance of the witness. So the request is the same, that a 60-day period should pass between the time the statement was disclosed to the Defence and the time the witness appears to testify in court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Of course, you are aware that this would entail a delay in the calling of the witnesses because that means that we would have to wait until, say, probably one month or even more, probably six weeks, before those particular witnesses are called by the Prosecution. If this is so, as I say, this will slow down the trial proceedings. But this is your position?

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Mr. President, we have a problem because we have about 34 statements submitted to us with delays, so this is a large number of witnesses. We have to prepare for them. Then there are another ten witnesses whose statements have not been disclosed, so we have to see whose interest is greater. Because what could occur is for witnesses to appear and testify about something we have no idea, and this is a very important issue. There is the possibility of a life sentence for our clients, and I think that we cannot take a leisurely attitude toward the Defence preparations, and I feel that the problem is that the Prosecution has taken a rather leisurely attitude towards this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. I will now turn to the Prosecution and ask them to clarify their position and to explain why there was such delay in the submission of witness statements and how this squares with the relevant Rules of Procedure; in particular, Rule 66(A)(ii), in its old version, because I feel that Mrs. Glumac is right in saying that we should apply the old version of our Rules because otherwise the new Rule would affect the rights of the Defence. Mr. Terrier?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Mr. President, at the outset, the Prosecution is of the opinion that it fully complied with its obligation of disclosure of all the exculpatory evidence it had in its possession, in keeping with your rules and Rules of Procedure and Evidence. Of course, we were bound by your decision issued on the 20th of May, 1998, and we are equally bound by Rule 66 of the Rules which, at the time when we had the pre-trial Status Conference, held that there had to be a 60-day time limit between the disclosure and the beginning of the hearing. Another part of the Rules is that copies of other Defence witness statements should be disclosed as soon as a decision to call them to testify is made. This (a) of Rule 66 is tantamount to saying that nobody wanted that the trial procedures should be made rigid before the trial proceedings were completed. The Prosecution, during the time reserved to it for the Prosecution's case, has the obligation of keeping -- of keeping working at finding elements which may be of use to the Tribunal, keep investigating on such matters. There is a first decision on the production of documents of the 16th of June, 1998 -- that was no problem because it was a date decided by your Trial Chamber. We made a choice which you may regret as Judges, but I would like to elucidate. We wanted to have a great number of testimonies under Rule 66, but also under Rule 68 of the Rules. It seemed to be of no problem to us to provide more witness statements to the Defence. That maybe was necessary due to the more limited number of witnesses we were going to call, so as to provide the Defence with all necessary information on the trial. And such testimonies, without going into the details of Rule 68 as to the disclosure of exculpatory evidence, such witness testimonies we thought might be of interest for the Defence in preparing their case. Our reading of Rule 68, which is very clear, which is absolutely indispensable in the Rules, is sometimes difficult to apply. It's hard to elucidate what an exculpatory piece of evidence is. We don't know what the Defence cases will be. Are they going to say that the accused were present in Ahmici on the 16th of April, 1993, or are they going to invoke another type of defence? So on the date ruled by your Court, we decided to disclose as great a number of statements as possible under Rule 66 and Rule 68, and in doing so, we believe that the Prosecution took due care of the interests of the Defence, provided the Defence with relevant and considerable material which made it possible for the Defence to prepare its case. There are other arguments made by the Defence. Some can be accounted for by the ruling of this Court aimed at protective measures for a number of witnesses and others are based on the Rule 66(A)(ii) which I read out a few minutes ago. Admittedly, a certain number of witnesses' names were not accompanied with the witness statements for the simple reason that we did not have the witness statements. If witnesses had provided witness statements we would, of course, disclose them to the Defence. So we believe that we complied with all the obligations we were under, under the Rules, and under the rulings by this Court. As to the motion filed before this Court today aiming at prohibiting the Prosecution from calling any witness whose name would not have been disclosed 60 days earlier, so this would mean that we could not call any new witness and this would be in patent violation of Rule 66(A)(i), and this is the reason why we believe that the Defence's motion should be denied by you. At any rate, if you were to rule against the Prosecution, you would be deprived of relevant information in this case, and you know from experience that it is when the time for the opening of the trial is drawing close, that it is then that important information is disclosed to the Prosecution, which then must submit it to your consideration; otherwise, it would be in violation of the fair administration of justice and in violation of the Rules.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, on behalf of the Chamber, I wish to put a few questions to you for clarification. There is a first problem dealing with figures. In a document recently filed with the Court, you state that you plan to call 71 witnesses. However, it appears from the motion filed by Mrs. Glumac that the witness statements which were gradually disclosed to the Defence amount to 82 or 81 witnesses. The first question we would like to put to you is to the effect of knowing who, among the 81 or 82 witnesses mentioned are the ones who are going to be called as Prosecution witnesses? We would like to understand why there is such a disparity in the figures. Another issue we would like to tackle: Did you disclose the witness statements of the 71 witnesses? If so, when did you do so? If I understood you adequately, you justify the fact that close to half of the witness statements of the witnesses you intend to call were disclosed once the 60-day time limit had come to an end. So legally speaking, what is your reason, your justification for the delay in submitting and disclosing the witness statements? You seem to invoke Rule 66(A)(ii), second part of the sentence, "Copies of the statements of additional Prosecution witnesses shall be made available to the Defence when a decision is made to call those witnesses" and, on the other hand, you also invoke Rule 68. "The Prosecutor shall, as soon as practicable, disclose to the Defence the existence of evidence known to the Prosecutor which, in any way, tends to suggest the innocence or mitigate the guilt of the accused or may affect the credibility of Prosecution evidence." In such a case, there is no time limit, and you argue that anyway, since evidence, exculpatory evidence, has to be disclosed 60 days before the trial begins, you are entitled to disclose the witness statements even after the 60-day time limit has elapsed. So the legal foundation you put forward is based on these two rules, and this is my first question to you. Did I interpret, did I understand you properly, and if it is so, you do realise that this would apply to just about half of the witnesses you intend to call, close to half of the witnesses. So there is no balance. Any accepted and agreed reading of the two Rules I have just mentioned are such that witness statements should be disclosed to the Defence within the 60-day time limit, and if there are any additional witnesses which would be few in number, if additional witnesses are discovered by the Prosecutor, the latter is entitled to disclose, even at the last minute, disclose the witness statements only recently discovered. Some kind of balance has to be maintained because this could be used as a technique to butt in at the last minute and to disclose those statements to the Defence only too late, and there the Defence is right, it would not have enough time to prepare its case, and the Defence is entitled to enough time so as to prepare its case in relation to witnesses whose statements have been produced at the very last minute. So I would like to have some explanations from you on these various points I have just mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: I shall endeavour to do so. As to the legal references or the legal foundation of our thesis, I have mentioned Rule 68 of the Rules on the disclosure of exculpatory evidence. I did so because I wanted to explain why we decided, back in June 1998, to produce a large number of witness statements to the Defence. There were among themselves statements of witnesses that we did then not plan to call to court, but we thought it was interesting for the Defence to know what was in the witness statements. But in order to use Rule 68, maybe we made a wrong choice, but I think it can be accounted for, we decided to disclose a large number of witness statements, and this was done under Rule 66 and Rule 68 of our Rules. You mentioned something that appeared to you as some delay in the disclosure of this information according to the rulings and according to the Rules. Let me say this: On the 3rd of August, we produced a list of 71 Prosecution witnesses to the Defence. We thought that these might be the witnesses that we may call to testify before you, and I can say already that out of the list of 71 witnesses we had drafted, we know already that seven will not appear. They decided not to appear for various reasons that I could explain to you, but this is to be inappropriate and out of place for the time being. Out of those, eight had not produced any witness statements, so we had nothing that we could disclose to the Defence. So out of the initial 71 witnesses whose names were disclosed to the Tribunal on the 3rd of August, 1998, there are only 56 witness statements. On the 16th of June, then on the 30th of June, as well as on the 17th of July, we disclosed a certain number of witness statements. I shall not mention those disclosed on the 16th of June because it doesn't seem to be challenged. As to the disclosure of the 30th of June, we disclosed 16 witness statements of which seven concerned witnesses for whom we had been granted an additional time limit by the Court. We regarded these witnesses as being possible Prosecution witnesses on the strength of the second part of Rule 66(A)(ii). For this same reason, we disclosed another 13 witness statements on the 17th of July. Last but not least, in the very first days of August, we produced and disclosed one last witness statement. So it's all a matter of appreciation as to the scope that can be given to that second part of Rule 66(A)(ii), and like other legal systems I am familiar with, with their own positive and negative sides, I want to mention that we did not want to have anything that would be fixed whilst the trial had not yet begun. We had to be able to find other new evidence until the trial would open so as to inform this Tribunal as comprehensively as possible as to the facts of this case. It would be regrettable if 60 days before the trial began, all the evidence, all the elements of a case file, were fixed once and for all. This would be regrettable for the Tribunal altogether. On the basis of the figures I have provided, I can say that the Prosecution has not made an excessive use of Rule 66(A)(ii). I believe that we used this Rule in a reasonable way and in a fair way towards the Defence. Should, of course, this Court rule otherwise, I shall comply with the ruling, but I think that I don't have any other things to say right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Of course, we agree with you as to the need not to predetermine too early in the piece how many witnesses will be called, but we need to find some kind of pragmatic solution. Hence, these two following questions. If my figures are right, 37 witness statements were disclosed to the Defence whilst the 60-day time limit had elapsed already. Thirty-seven minus eight, because these were the statements of protected witnesses, and, as you said, you were authorised to disclose those witness statements with some delay. Remain 29 witness statements. First question: Out of the 29 witnesses, how many of them are Defence witnesses governed by Rule 68 of the Rules? How much of it is exculpatory evidence? Second question: Out of the 29 witnesses, how many do we have who are among the 56 witnesses which you intend to call and whose statements you have? I am mentioning 56 because I am taking 71 minus seven, minus eight. So out of the 71 witnesses, we have to take seven and then eight out, remain 56. So we have the figure of 56 and now we have 29 witness statements. We would like to have the proper ratio to put us in a position to rule adequately. So what did you do? Did you use, if not abuse this liberty, did you have a sort of extensive interpretation of this last part of Rule 68(A)(ii)?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: I understand your concerns, Your Honour. Let me explain the matter of these figures. As far as the 29 witness statements are concerned, you are right, Your Honour, they were disclosed after the time limit had elapsed and outside of the Court rulings. I note that eight of the witnesses have not produced witness statements. We are not in a position to disclose those witness statements to the Defence. So we should take these eight witnesses with no witness statements out of the 29. You wished to know, Mr. President, which of the 37 witness statements disclosed in June, on the 16th of June, 1998, which, among those witness statements, had been disclosed with some delay and how many of them could be justified by Rule 68. I say that among those witness statements disclosed out of the time limit, none of them is based on Rule 68. All the disclosure to be carried out under Rule 68 has been done, and we did not find any other element that could be regarded as exculpatory evidence. If we had, of course, we would have disclosed in keeping with the Rule. I am not right now in a position of informing you any further. If you wanted any more refined calculations, maybe we could have some time in order to do so, but presently, this is all I can say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Last question: What is your position in respect of the Defence motion as argued orally this morning? It may be that I had failed to understand the written motion, so this is to the effect of having the testimonies of witnesses postponed if their witness statements fail to be disclosed within the time limit of 60 days. But if I understood the Defence right, the Defence said that it is not asking to preclude such testimonies even if the witness statements were disclosed with delay. They only want to have a 60-day time limit which they can enjoy, which would mean that the witnesses could be called only in three to four weeks' time. What is your position as to the motion argued by Mrs. Glumac?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: I had some trouble and difficulty in understanding the accurate meaning of the Defence motion. If the Defence motion ends at requesting that the calling of testimony with examination-in-chief and cross-examination by the Defence would be postponed for more than 60 days following the disclosure of the witness statements, this is contrary to justice, in my submission, and also in violation of the Rules. However, if the Defence should wish to have the opportunity to receive the opportunity from the Chamber to proceed to the cross-examination of a witness at a later date, the witness could come and be heard and be examined in chief, and as long as there were good reasons to do so, the Defence could proceed to the cross-examination only later on, maybe when it comes to the Defence case, and I think that this could be perfectly all right for us and the fears of the Defence might be allayed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I think that Judge May wanted to ask a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Terrier, yes, the essence of the problem is that the Defence should have proper time to prepare. Trial by ambush is unacceptable, but at the moment, I haven't -- it may be that I have overlooked it -- a list of when statements were disclosed. Now, it may be that the problem can be overcome if sufficient time has been given for the Defence to prepare the particular witnesses, prepare their cross-examination. Obviously, they must have time to do that. But what I don't think we have is a list of the witnesses with a list of when the statements were disclosed. Could I refer you, please, to the order of witnesses and estimated length of examination-in-chief which you produced on the 3rd of August? Registry page 2053. Where we have your list of witnesses, I take it from the way its described, in the order in which you propose to call them, starting with Mr. Watters. Now, I think what would be helpful to me so that I can try and judge that is to know which of those witnesses you now propose not to call so that we do not have to be troubled with that, but also to know when these statements of these witnesses were disclosed. For instance, those witnesses who you propose to call in the next day or two during the course of the next week, were they disclosed within the normal Rules or have they recently been disclosed, in which case it may be right not to call them at that stage? Can you assist us to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Your Honours, of course we shall submit to you a more precise account out of the list of 71 witnesses filed on the 3rd of August. We are going to provide you with the exact dates when the witness statements were disclosed to the Defence. But I do insist those of the witnesses who never produced any witness statements do not fall under the obligation of disclosure because there is nothing to disclose, and we know -- for some of them we know that they will not be called. Eight witnesses did not make any witness statements, seven will not come. Well, this is what we know today. As far as this week is concerned, I can tell you, and this will be checked very closely, but I don't think this will be challenged by the Defence, I do believe that all the witness statements were indeed disclosed to the Defence counsel; therefore, there should not be any problem for this week. But let me add that even for the witnesses to be called this week, we are not yet absolutely sure of the order of witnesses. We don't know whether the order that was scheduled on the 3rd of August can be totally adhered to. There are specific constraints under which we operate. We are talking about events that took place 1500 kilometres away from here five years ago, some people moved out, left the country; others are under family or professional obligations, they have commitments, and we have to make sure that we do take their wishes into account. So please do not believe that this is a sign of inconsistency or of flippancy on the part of the Prosecution, but it may well be that at times the order in which the witnesses may be called will not be the order that had been initially scheduled. It may well be that some of the witnesses mentioned in the list of whom we think will be willing to come might, in the end, decide not to testify before the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Terrier, will you produce for us, please, a schedule setting out when it was that the witness statements were disclosed, and it might be helpful if that was done in the order of the witnesses which you set out on the 3rd of August. There is one further matter I want to raise, if I may, and it's this: That you made the point, Mr. Terrier, that it was not clear from the Defence as to whether it was admitted that the accused were in Ahmici on the 16th of April. In fact, in the case of one accused, it is admitted, although it said he was in the shelter, and if I have read that right, that's in the case of Vlatko Kupreskic, but I think I'm right in saying that no other accused has addressed this important point. Now, if it is to be suggested that an accused was not in Ahmici that day, then clearly that would constitute an alibi, and that would require, or requires under the Rules, disclosure before the trial, and perhaps I am addressing the Defence through you. Were it suggested that any accused was not in Ahmici that day, that should be promptly disclosed, but one must take it from the absence of disclosure that, in fact, that is not the case. But it would be helpful to know what the defence is on that particular point. One accused has made his position clear, and it seems to me the others should do so too.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: In respect of the two questions raised by Judge May, I say that shortly within the recess granted, we shall communicate to you the dates of disclosure for those witnesses. When it comes to the defence of alibi as invoked by Mr. Kupreskic, and Rule 67 indeed, there is a need to communicate the intention of having witnesses appear on this defence of alibi, and we did not receive any other notification from any other Defence counsel for other accused. We conclude, therefore, that they themselves could testify on a special defence. This is the third sub-rule of Rule 67. But other witnesses could not be called on their behalf. But I believe that I noted in the statements disclosed this morning or a few days ago, I noted that several of the accused did not challenge or deny that they were present in Ahmici on the 16th of April. They do challenge the arguments raised by the Prosecution, but they do not challenge the fact that they were present in Ahmici. But I do believe that the Defence could more adequately than I do express their views on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I wonder whether we can, before moving on to other items and before we take a break, we should break at around 11.00, whether I could turn to Mrs. Glumac and ask whether she would like to comment on the response given by the Prosecution to this particular item. Let us leave aside now the defence, the alibi question, because on that particular point, I should turn to Mr. Krajina. Please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: We have responded in our brief saying that at the critical time our clients were indeed in Ahmici. As for the comments of the Prosecution, I think that he is not quite clear on the dates when the statements were disclosed. I have checked the dates and put them down and I can supply those dates to the Court. The Prosecutor has not disputed those dates. It seems to us that the Prosecutor says that he doesn't have statements for eight witnesses but, according to our count, it's ten, so it seems to me that it is quite the same to them whether it is eight or ten. I think that we must take care that the evidence is presented to the Defence correctly. It is not proper to act in this way. All these are witnesses on the Prosecutor's list. If I understood him well, he said that at first the statements of witnesses were given that they do not intend to call so as to give us an overall picture of the situation and that they did not submit statements of the witnesses they do intend to call. But that is obstruction of the Defence. So how can we prepare our defence in this way? That is what I heard at least being said by the Prosecutor, and I do feel that that is a violation of our rights. I agree that we should not freeze the process of presentation of evidence, but the question is, what has been happening in the meantime? There were no new investigations. These statements are all several years old. They are not the product of any current investigation. Therefore, I feel that the explanations given by the Prosecutor are not acceptable. In addition to my motion, I had intended to attach these dates so that the Trial Chamber should have an idea of the way in which the Prosecution behaved. I am not trying to say that anyone is intentionally wasting time. We do indeed want an expeditious trial but also a fair one, because that is our right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me just clarify one point -- yes, please, Mr. Radovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: In connection with the question of special defence and the defence of alibi, we know that we are obliged to disclose such a defence promptly, but in this case, that point will not be disputed, whether our clients were in Ahmici as an area. But what is disputed is whether they were in a spot where they shouldn't have been or somewhere else, and that is my reply to the question put by Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes. Let us leave aside for one second the question of alibi because we have to now adjourn. It is clear that now the Prosecutor will provide the Defence and the Court a list of 71 names and he will specify there when the relevant statements have been produced. The eight or ten names of the witnesses for whom no statements have been produced, and also the list of those witnesses, out of those 71 witnesses who have dropped out already, so that we can make up our minds and decide on this matter. Let me just clarify one point, probably due to a misunderstanding because of interpretation problems. Mrs. Glumac said that the Prosecution does not intend to provide to the Defence some statements of witnesses. Actually, the Prosecutor said that for eight witnesses they do not have statements. They're not withholding those statements, they simply don't have those statements available, so that's why -- but also for those witnesses, we would like to have a proper indication of their names so that when we resume at 11.30 or 11.35, probably the Prosecutor will be in a position to pass on to us and give to the Defence this particular list. I think we should now adjourn and discuss the issue of alibi later on because I see that some Defence counsel are keen to address this particular point. Let me say that I hope that by half past 12.00, when we have to adjourn, I hope that we will be in a position to go through various procedural matters, and this afternoon at two o'clock when we reconvene, we should be able to quickly deal with the housekeeping matters and then start with the opening statement of the Prosecutor so that we proceed in a quick way. I now suggest that we adjourn for 30 minutes. So we will rise now. We will come back at 11.32 sharp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I must apologise for the delay, but I understand the Prosecutor needed some time. I wonder whether the Prosecutor is now in a position to give us these documents; otherwise, we can move on to other matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Mr. President, yes, we are in a position to provide you with the document, but there are other matters that maybe we should look into which could give me enough time to check the various pieces of information and draw up a summary. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Then may I suggest that we move on to our next item, namely, the issues which were raised -- some of the issues, legal issues, which were raised in the motion filed by the counsel for Vlatko Kupreskic. This motion for the withdrawal of the indictment. There are some particular matters which I think have been caused mainly by a misunderstanding. May I draw the attention of Defence counsel to page 5, paragraphs 19 through 22, of their motion, and I would like to ask Defence counsel to clarify their position on this particular matter because, as I say, I have the feeling that all the issues raised by Mr. Krajina are probably due to some misunderstanding concerning the position of the Prosecution. May I ask Mr. Krajina to come back and dwell upon those paragraphs, 19 through -- well, say, 24?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: With your leave, Your Honour, may my colleague Par explain this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but we have a problem with Mr. Par because -- this is a question which I intended to raise later on -- within the framework of what I have called the housekeeping matters; namely, the right of audience of Mr. Par. Now, Mr. Par is a legal assistant and, as such, he has no right of audience. He can sit here in the courtroom, but he has no right of audience. Since, therefore, this problem has cropped up now, I will deal with it right away because I understand that Mr. Krajina had requested that the position of Mr. Par be upgraded to that of a co-counsel. A co-counsel is entitled to address the Court, in addition of course, to sitting in court. Now, on this matter, the Trial Chamber has already come to a decision based on the following elements: First of all, a ruling was made by Trial Chamber II both in Tadic and in Kupreskic to the effect that whenever the lead counsel does not have any command of one of the two working languages of our Tribunal, French or English, he may suggest that a co-counsel be appointed, of course on condition that the co-counsel has full command and is fluent in one of the two working languages. We have to stick to this ruling, and for this purpose, the Trial Chamber has requested the Registry, which has the final say on this matter, as you know, to let us know what their position was. The position of the Registry is that, according to the Registrar and the Deputy Registrar, Mr. Par does not meet the linguistic requirements which are laid down I think, if I am correct, in Rule 14 of the relevant document. I have got this document somewhere, but I will dig it out in a few minutes, because there it is stated that the counsel must -- the lead counsel must be fluent in one of the two languages. So this is the position of the Registry, and the Registry, however, has suggested that this position should be, in a way, scrutinised by the Trial Chamber, which will eventually decide upon this matter. This is our second element, the second element we have decided to take into account. The third element is the judicial practice of the other Trial Chambers. They have consistently decided that either the leading counsel or the co-counsel must meet the requirements laid down in that particular provision, Article 14, and therefore, if the Registrar or the Deputy Registrar feel that those requirements are not fulfilled, the suggested co-counsel may not take up the task of co-counsel but may be given the position of legal assistant. Therefore, I suggest -- legal assistant, yes. We have decided that Mr. Par should be given the position of legal assistant, and therefore, Mr. Krajina is entitled to address the Court on any question relating to their accused. This being so, I wonder whether Mr. Krajina is in a position to address the item we were discussing; namely, the paragraphs I had mentioned of their motion. I am referring, of course, to the motion filed on the 27th of July suggesting that the indictment against Vlatko Kupreskic should be withdrawn and suggesting also that a separate hearing should be scheduled. As you know, Judge Mumba had already issued an order on this particular motion; however, in that order, as I reminded you this morning, in that order, Judge Mumba, acting on behalf of the Trial Chamber, decided that any problems, procedural problems, which were outstanding should be addressed in court this morning. So I wonder whether again -- I turn to Mr. Krajina. I would like to ask him whether he would be prepared to do so or whether he would like to deal with this matter this afternoon?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: Your Honour, since my colleague Par prepared to present the argument, may I be allowed to respond to your questions this afternoon? I don't know whether I understood well, Mr. President, whether this applies to your decision regarding our subsequent request for the appointment of Mr. Par as co-counsel because certain circumstances have changed regarding his command of an official language, and subsequently we addressed the Registry in writing and received a positive response from the Registry but, of course, the final decision was left with the Trial Chamber. Therefore, I didn't understand quite well whether the Trial Chamber is familiar with this most recent opinion of the Registry regarding this matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: No, we received from the Registrar a letter, which I have here in front of me, where he stated that actually, according to the Registrar, those requirements are not met; however, that, of course, the Trial Chamber would have final say on this matter. We decided to stick to the judicial practice of other Trial Chambers as well as to the ruling made by our Chamber in Tadic and Kupreskic; and therefore, to assign Mr. Par the role and the status of a legal assistant. This applies also to any future question and to your motion. Of course, I am ready to comply with your request that you should address this issue this afternoon so as to have enough time to prepare on this particular matter. Now, let us -- if, meanwhile, the Prosecutor has -- are you in a position to come back to that particular point, or shall we move on to -- well, I could ask the Prosecutor a question about the two ex parte motions filed recently, and we feel that it is probably not necessary that the Prosecutor should present oral argument on those motions because they are quite clear and we may make a ruling on them without hearing oral argument. However, if the Prosecutor is willing and prepared and wishes to present oral argument, of course, we would hold ex parte proceedings. What is your position?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Mr. President, it is up to you. I do believe that the motions are clear in themselves. Should the Court wish to receive additional explanations, we are willing to provide the Court with them, but I think we are in the hands of the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: All right. So we will decide on this matter, if possible, at lunch time, and we may now move on to two issues raised this morning in addition to the various items that I had set out in my introduction. One issue is that of protective measures was raised by the Prosecutor, and the other problems were raised by Defence counsel: One, the restoration of documents and property of Vlatko Kupreskic and the second item was the specialist medical examination, again of Mr. Vlatko Kupreskic. Could we start with the protective measures? I wonder whether the Prosecutor could briefly deal with this item so that we may then afterwards, if need be, hear the Defence counsel and move on?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We wish to address the way this Chamber wishes the parties to proceed in respect of protective measures which will be asked for regarding a number of witnesses. We know already that some witnesses, who all reside in Bosnia, will ask for protective measures, and based on that request, will put forward arguments that appear to be extremely well-founded. For instance, some witnesses have professional or social dealings with members from the other community and wish that their contribution to the ICTY remains as low profile as possible. The Tribunal is well-aware of the situation prevailing in Bosnia, still prevailing in Bosnia and Central Bosnia. It is a very unstable, precarious situation. There are acute tensions still between the communities. Therefore, our requests for protective measures are required by factual circumstances. We need to ensure the protection of the witnesses as ruled by the Statute but also by several Rules of Procedure and Evidence. So a pragmatic suggestion, in order to waste as little time as possible and to work to the satisfaction of all parties, is as such: When and if the Defence agrees to the requested protective measures, alteration of the voice, distorting the images, if such measures are agreed to by the Defence, the Chamber would not have to make any ruling on such measures. It may be different if, as provided by the Rules, the Chamber has to give reasoned motives for the protective measures. This should happen in closed session. This will happen only very rarely. I don't know as yet whether we shall ask hearings to be held in closed sessions, in-camera. It may well be the case, but I am not in a position to say when the Prosecution may have to ask for closed sessions. As to the witnesses due to appear this week, we ask for minimum protective measures, the voice should be distorted, so should the images, and we may ask some other minor protective measures. The only request I wish to formulate is that the Court should tell us which time limits to apply for the request of such protective measures, whether they are accepted or not accepted by the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I wonder whether the Defence counsel has anything to say on this particular matter. Our conclusion would be -- I have quickly consulted with my two fellow Judges -- and we feel that, to respond to the request of the Prosecutor, of course our philosophy is that all the protective measures requested by other parties should be accepted to the extent that they do not limit the rights of the Defence, which are sacrosanct. First point. So, therefore, we intend to be quite generous in complying with requests designed to protect witnesses. The second point is that, of course, we can't make a decision, a blanket decision, but any decision must be made on a case-by-case basis, it goes without saying. Third point, from the viewpoint of practicality, I would suggest that if the parties are agreeable, that probably a day before a witness is called the party calling the witness should propose to the Trial Chamber the sort of protective measures to be taken. We will ask the other party whether they are agreeable, and then we will grant, if need be, the requested protective measure. Is it feasible, if you say a day before a witness is called, you suggest to the Court that you would like the particular witness to enjoy particular protective measures, we could make up our mind right away after consulting with the other party. What is your position on this?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Quite, Mr. President. I see absolutely no difficulty in doing so. The Chamber may wish one of the Defence counsel to be appointed as our counterpart in such questions and we could, before addressing the Court, turn to the representative of the Defence counsel to see whether they agree with the requested protective measures so as to duly inform the Court. But I think it might be good to have one such member of the Defence counsel to be appointed for the purpose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I think that is quite sensible, what you have suggested. Actually, we had already -- remember, we had thought of coordinating counsel, and this morning I reminded you that we are very keen to know whether a coordinating counsel has been appointed by the various counsel. We raised this issue some time ago. I remember that Defence -- one or two Defence counsel said they were not able to appoint just one coordinating counsel but they preferred to have two counsel, one speaking on behalf of a particular group, I think you mentioned, the Zagreb group, is it? Am I correct? And the other one, I don't remember which sort of group, linked to an area or to a city. I wonder, since we are dealing with this matter, it is a matter which I intended to raise this afternoon within the framework of the so-called "housekeeping matters," I wonder if you could tell me whether or not you have agreed upon a particular Defence counsel to act on behalf of all of them, to discuss all these procedural matters, in particular, to act in contact with the Prosecutor so that we can speed up practical matters and deal with them as quickly as possible. May I ask one of you to respond? I thought Mr. Radovic. I don't remember. I think Mr. Radovic, were you -- can I ask one of you just to remind us of what you had decided or whether or not you have changed your mind?

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, we have decided nothing regarding this matter. If it is necessary to appoint a coordinator, then I would ask for a short recess for us to make a kind of brief elections to see who we could appoint?

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Mr. President, I feel that Petar Pavkovic has already been appointed coordinator. This is something that has gone down in the record, and I think that colleague Radovic was the author of that proposal or, rather, of that appointment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes, I think your recollection seems to be correct, and Judge May ... 15th of May. I think since there may be hesitations, of course, you are fully entitled to have some time to discuss again this matter and come back to us maybe this afternoon. Is it fine with you if, say, you let us know this afternoon at 2.00 when we reconvene so you have plenty of time at lunch time. We tend, I'm afraid, to work at lunch time, both parties and the Judges. I'm afraid it's a bit taxing. All right. So much for the protective measures. We could probably quickly move on to the question raised by counsel for Vlatko Kupreskic about the restoration of documents and property belonging to Vlatko Kupreskic and since the issue was quickly raised this morning, I think by Mr. Krajina, I wonder whether the Prosecutor is in a position to state their stand on this particular point. Mr. Moskowitz?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. We filed, I think it was on May 20th, pursuant to this Court's order, a detailed accounting of the briefcase, and we have looked high and low for documents as described by Mr. Kupreskic as being in that briefcase. To the best of our ability, we have not found those documents. There was an extensive inventory done, there was a re-check done, there was an attempt to actually have Mr. Kupreskic look through the briefcase himself, but the briefcase had been sent back to Bosnia by the time that could take place. So it is our view and our position that those documents were not in the briefcase when we obtained them from SFOR back in 1997.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you, since you are now addressing the Court, also deal with the question of the specialist medical examination, the other issue raised this morning by Mr. Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: May I have a moment to consult? It is our position that we do not object to that kind of examination, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Krajina, may I ask you to comment?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: Mr. President, first of all, may I thank you for putting on the agenda these two issues which we consider to be very important for the Defence of the accused Mr. Kupreskic. As for the restoration of documents contained in the briefcase when the accused Kupreskic was arrested, may I very briefly provide some explanations in connection with this problem? We had several contacts with the Office of the Prosecutor, and, as you know, this was discussed at the Status Conference held on the 15th of May this year, and there is a ruling of the Trial Chamber explicitly instructing that all objects seized from the accused have to be restored to the accused. The Prosecutor's Office has denied the existence of 14 documents, as my learned friend claims now as well, that they were not in the briefcase at the time that it was seized from the accused. In our submission of the 2nd of June this year, which we addressed to the Trial Chamber, we continue to allege that the objects, that the contested objects were indeed in the briefcase. They were prepared and put in the briefcase by our client because he intended to use them for his defence in the Tribunal. He kept for himself copies of all those documents, and they are still in his possession. Why do we keep pressing this issue? Because we wish to avoid the unnecessary effort that tracing those documents would entail and because we fear that in the course of that process, if we were to present copies of those documents in court, they may be challenged, and that is why we keep insisting that those originals need to be found and restored to the accused. The instructions given by the Trial Chamber to the Prosecutor to find and restore those documents says that the Prosecutor was also obliged to prepare an inventory of all the objects found in the briefcase and how, upon his arrest. I must repeat that the report submitted by the Prosecutor on the 20th of May, '98, does not contain such an inventory, such a list, with data on documents found in the briefcase, and because no such list has been submitted, the instructions of the Trial Chamber have not been followed, and all we hear now from the Prosecution is simply that those documents were not to be found in the briefcase. Our submission was that this problem could be tackled in two ways: either by making an inventory list, which probably exists, or by interviewing the persons who had any contact with the briefcase before it reached the Prosecution and the Tribunal. In that way, we could establish the chain of custody or, the alternative would be for the Defence to be allowed to use copies of those documents in the course of the presentation of its case in court on the condition that they should not be challenged. We are referring to copies only of those documents that were contained in the briefcase. That is why, in view of the fact that we still haven't received a final answer regarding our motion, we appeal to the Trial Chamber to make a ruling on this matter. A second point that we would like to raise has to do with our request for specialist examinations of our client. Vlatko Kupreskic, according to available medical documentation, is disabled 100 per cent because of a congenital heart condition and because of surgery that he underwent on his heart. That is why, for seven months now, the time that he has been in detention, we have been asking that the appropriate experts, cardiologists, should examine our client and file their reports on their findings because by staying in detention -- and we know what that means for people with a heart condition -- he is frequently in a stressful condition; and in our request, we asked permission for a specialist to examine our client, and we proposed the names of university professors, specialists. However, the Registrar did not accept this but notified us that Mr. Kupreskic would be examined by a Dr. Deichman of the Netherlands, a cardiologist; however, to date no such examination has taken place, nor have we been notified in any way why this has not been done. We must also point out in this Trial Chamber that we are concerned for the condition of our client and, as his Defence counsel and as human beings, we would not like to accept any responsibility should anything happen to him while in detention. In connection with this health problem of our client, we have also submitted a request to the management of the detention unit to allow the accused Vlatko time in the fresh air that is double the amount that people in good health are given. We have not received official permission for this either, though I must say that the unit management has informally accepted this request of ours. Also, we have requested that during the breaks in the trial, the accused should be allowed to go outside the booths envisaged for the accused which obviously lack fresh air so that he be allowed to spend the time during the break in another room with fresh air. This request has not been responded to either to date, and we appeal to the Trial Chamber to make an appropriate ruling on this matter too. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. All right. Let me start with the question of restoration of documents and property to Mr. Vlatko Kupreskic. Actually, I understand 14 documents are missing and, of course, they can't be found, and we don't doubt the good faith of those who seized those documents. Probably they got lost. Therefore, we feel that the Defence counsel is entitled to use copies of those 14 documents and the Prosecutor will not, of course, be allowed to challenge the authenticity of those copies. It goes without saying that we will take into account the fact that we will be using copies. As for the specialist medical examination, the Trial Chamber fully shares the concern of Defence counsel, and we will direct the Registrar to ensure that Mr. Vlatko Kupreskic be visited by one or two cardiologists as soon as possible. Actually, I hope in the next few days. I fully share your views that it is crucial for the accused to be duly examined by one or more specialists. This is a matter which, of course, comes within the purview of the Registrar, but we will today ask the Registrar to put in hand all the necessary measures. As for the question of fresh air, again, we also share your concern. We feel this is quite an appropriate request, but again, this is a matter which must be decided upon by the Registrar. We will ask the Registrar to see to it that the accused, if possible, enjoy some fresh air in the appropriate times instead of being locked in some closed rooms. I think we have disposed of this matter. Since we still have some time, I wonder whether the Prosecutor is now in a position to let us know about the list of witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Mr. President. I am referring to this list of 71 witness names which was filed with the Tribunal in the beginning of August in keeping with the wish you expressed during the Status Conference. I note that ten and not eight, as I mistakenly mentioned earlier on, that ten witnesses have not produced any written statement, which means that we cannot disclose any of those statements under Rule 66. So this was a very accurate observation by the Defence. We are dealing with ten and not eight witnesses, having not produced any statement. Following the 16th of June, the witness statements of 38 witnesses were disclosed to the Defence. On the 30th of June, 14 witness statements were disclosed, among which there were statements of seven witnesses for which postponement of the disclosure had been granted by the Tribunal. Following the 17th of July, the statements of five witnesses were disclosed to the Defence, and on the 5th of August, three witnesses were notified to the Defence. I add that in compliance with the Court orders, one witness statement was disclosed on the 10th of August. This was one of the last witnesses for whom protective measures had been granted by this Court. So if you quickly sum up all this, you find out that out of the 71 witnesses mentioned in the list, minus the seven who will not testify and possibly additional witnesses not willing to testify, we have 15 names for which disclosure will be provided once the -- although the time limit has elapsed, this is based on 66(A)(ii) because it appeared that they were necessary witnesses for the Prosecution, although the time limit had elapsed. This process of disclosure is sometimes inevitably confused. Some disclosure took place within the time limits, and for some of the witnesses disclosed within the 60-day time limit on the 16th of June, we may have additional statements, but they were already disclosed to the Defence. Most of the time we were dealing with witness statements that we had but had only in Serbo-Croatian. Translation had to be carried out which necessitated further time limits. As a result, with regard to some witness statements, they were disclosed past the 16th of June, past the 60-day time limit. I think this will not be challenged by the Defence. As to the additional witness statements disclosed, we are only dealing with statements that we wanted to disclose but there was no additional input compared with the previous witness statements. It was for the sake of thoroughness and comprehensiveness that we wanted to disclose them. But they were names that we didn't have in our files. So these are all the data relating to disclosure. Once again I repeat that we have the feeling that we did not exceed our rights under the Rules, we complied to the letter and the spirit of the Rules, we equally complied with the Court orders, the 15 witnesses that were belatedly disclosed or were disclosed past the 60-day time limit had elapsed, were disclosed belatedly because of the investigating effort that we were still carrying out, although the 60 days had elapsed. We had the feeling that the Office of the Prosecutor and its representatives fully complied with the spirit and the letter of the Tribunal and the Court orders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Two things: Could we have the list that is in the document filed on the 3rd of August, the order of appearance, the order in which you intend to call the various witnesses so we could have, in addition to the information already provided, an indication of the time when you disclosed the statements to the Defence? Could you tell us as well who are the witnesses who will not come to testify and who are the 15 you mentioned? Because we wanted to address this matter during the lunch break, and it might be useful to have the said list, say, in half an hour. That would be very useful. But we have something else that bothers us. I mentioned that with my colleagues over the break. There are ten witnesses for whom you did not disclose any statements because there aren't any statements, but the Defence is entitled to prepare for cross-examination, and we hold the view that the Defence is entitled to at least a short summary concerning each witness, concerning also the topics addressed by the witnesses during their testimonies. This is essential. Failing that, the Defence is not in a position to prepare its case and to defend their clients, so we would like to have at least a summary of the essential points dealt with during testimony.
