The Defence, otherwise, could not know what you would have to cross-examine upon. Is the Prosecution in a position to disclose such a summary for each of the ten witnesses concerned to the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: If the Chamber expresses such a wish, we shall, of course, comply. I do understand the reasons why you formulate such a wish, you express concern because there is no Rule, no provision dealing with this. Nowhere is it said in the Rules that this should be disclosed, the names should be disclosed to the Defence; no special, no specific measure is provided for either party because we might find ourselves in the same situation when the Defence case comes. Nothing is said as to the need and the obligation to supply the other party, the opposing party, with the gist of such witness statements. It may well be a good cause to adopt, but with a proviso that it may be difficult to be totally accurate and comprehensive in respect of a testimony that we intend to provide the Court with just on the basis of hypothesis of investigation carried out by the Prosecution. Say if we call a specialist in demography before this Court, we know, obviously, which topic we shall ask him to deal with and it is therefore easy not to provide the answers to the questions to the Defence but at least to provide the Defence with the gist of the questions that are likely to be asked of the witness. However, if we ask a specialist in ethnology before the Court and we ask that person to express their views on the living conditions, on the relationships within the various ethnic communities before 1992, in '92, and past '92, in '93, it will be difficult for us to tell you what the gist will be of such testimony. It could only be limited to what I have said myself right now. So we are perfectly aware of the concerns and the wishes expressed by the Tribunal. We shall endeavour, within reasonable limits, to provide a summary for those witnesses who have not provided any written statements. I hope that this commitment is in compliance with your wishes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes, quite, but I don't quite agree with you with your legal interpretation. There are provisions in the Rules, there is a fundamental principle anchored in the Statute, Article 21(4)(B) every accused has the right to have anything that is necessary for the preparation of their defence, and if he wants to prepare his defence, the accused has to know what the topics will be that will be addressed. So we have a very solid legal foundation ensuring the protection of the accused's rights but, on the other hand, I wish to insist on something that we already mentioned in a prior hearing when it comes to expert witnesses. Let us attempt to have as few of them as possible. Let us not fall again into this trend that we notice from the Office of the Prosecutor, which is to call too many witnesses. I think we should focus on the allegations formulated by the Prosecution against the accused. We have to limit, as much as we can, the number of expert witnesses who are not going to say anything in relation to the accused. I am aware of the legal issues of crimes against humanity, of persecution. The Prosecutor, therefore, has to insist on some general facts to establish the framework, and then, at a later stage, to focus on the charges pressed against the accused. But we have got to focus on the charges rather than on the general topics like demography. So let's try to avoid too general issues. For instance, the relationship between two ethnic groups causes me to wonder whether it would be appropriate. Of course, you are free to call any witnesses you may wish to call, but we have to try and limit, to the best extent possible, the number of witnesses, especially if such witnesses are not relevant to the charges or not crucial in relation of those charges.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: I do quite understand what you are saying. I was just mentioning a specialist in demography by way of an example. I don't think it will be necessary. Let me just say this: The Prosecution does not intend to cause delay or digressions that will be unnecessary to the Tribunal. We want to focus as much as possible on the charges. However, we do wish to provide necessary explanations as to the circumstances of the crimes indicted in the indictment as well as on the general circumstances prevailing at the time of the facts. We hope to be in a position to provide the Judges with all the points that are necessary for determination of the issue. This may be ambitious, but I can tell you that we do not want this trial to be unduly long.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I think we are coming close to the end of this hearing. We are going to suspend our work. We are going to start at 2.00 sharp, and I hope that, within the next ten to fifteen minutes, you will be in a position to provide us with a relevant document, and I hope that we will not devote more than three-quarters of an hour to these preliminary matters in the early afternoon, including the housekeeping matters that I would like to deal with the two parties. I would like to move as fast as we can to the opening statement by the Prosecution, so as to open and start the trial proper. But you want to ask a question, Judge May, don't you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Terrier, have you the document there that we were talking about with the witnesses and the dates of disclosure? Is that really it? Behind you there is a document being waved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: All right. I think probably we can, although this is not complete, we can use it for the purpose of our ruling. We will now adjourn and reconvene at 2.00 sharp. We will start with the Defence counsel. We hope to hear from Defence counsel, to hear the name of the coordinating counsel. Then we will ask Mr. Krajina to elaborate on the motion concerning Vlatko Kupreskic and we will move on to the few practical housekeeping matters. After that, I hope even before our break, which will be at 3.30, I think, I hope that the Prosecutor will probably start with his opening statement, which I assume will not be very long because we have already been provided a detailed pre-trial brief, which is quite useful, and then we can move on to various matters -- or witnesses. This afternoon, I will ask the Defence counsel whether they wish to make an opening statement at this stage or whether they prefer to make their opening statement at the end of the Prosecution case. This is for you to decide, and you will let me know this afternoon. So we may adjourn now, and we will reconvene at 2.00 sharp. 19 20 21 22 23 24 25 --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.35 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Mr. President, may I ask you that we consider the question of alibi referred to by Judge May, and at the same time I shall request to speak on the issue if possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes, this will be done in a few minutes. Let us first of all deal with other matters. First of all, I would like to read out the ruling on the motion filed on the 13th of August, 1998 by Defence counsel for Zoran and Mirjan Kupreskic. It is as follows: The Trial Chamber decides that those Prosecution witnesses whose statements have been disclosed to the Defence after the 16th of June '98, may be called by the Prosecutor only 30 days after such disclosure. This ruling also applies to the ten witnesses for whom the Prosecutor shall provide a summary of evidence, whereas it does not apply to the eight witnesses for whom the Trial Chamber ordered protective measures. Now, we will issue by tomorrow morning orders concerning the two ex parte motions filed by the Prosecutor. We have already deliberated on that matter and those two questions, and we may now move on to -- first of all, let me ask whether the various Defence counsel have appointed a coordinating counsel. May I ask Mr. Pavkovic to tell me whether he has been confirmed as coordinating counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, members of the Trial Chamber, by unanimous decision by my learned colleagues, I shall in the future present the positions which my colleagues feel I should present as our common positions. Of course, I must underline that that does not affect the core of the Defence of each one of us, because we are all defending separate accused, and then they will separately present their arguments. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: That's good news. Now, by the way, as for the definition of coordinating counsel and his tasks, or her tasks, may I refer you to the guidelines we issued, guidelines for the trial, letter A, number 1: Defence counsel are to agree to appoint from their number a coordinating counsel whose role will be to address the Court and communicate with the Prosecution on those matters in which the co-accused share a joint position. This is in line with what you just said, so we are very pleased that all Defence counsel unanimously agreed to appoint you as coordinating counsel. I think we shall now move on this question of alibi, the alibi defence, and I would like to ask Mr. Susak to address this item.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Mr. President, the question of alibi is a difficult issue, both for me and for my client, Drago Josipovic. Namely, in the indictment Drago Josipovic is charged, as are the other accused, of criminal offences from the period of October '92 to April '93. And I think it is impossible for the accused to refer to an alibi, because the Prosecutor charges him of having been there, moving around in his neighbourhood, near his house, where his family lives, and so on. However, on that same indictment, Marinko Katava was charged in the same way as the other accused. And he referred to the Defence of alibi only for the date of the 16th of April. And after that the Prosecutor withdrew the indictment against him. This fact confused my client, as it did me, and I don't know how we can refer to an alibi when he is charged with offences throughout this period. That is one point. My second point is: Could the Prosecutor assist the Defence in such a way as to specify the criminal offence? Because the indictment says that on the 16th of April, eight villages were attacked, and the town of Vitez, and my client was a member of the village guard; so the question is could he have organised and planned an attack on such a wide area, the more so as he was not a member of the civilian authorities, he was not a member of the party, nor was he a member of the active military force. Therefore, I think that the Prosecutor should assist us and shorten these proceedings, because in that case we would need to hear only fewer, fewer witnesses. So, could the Prosecutor specify where and when Drago Josipovic committed the offences, what acts he committed and what were the consequences of those acts. That is my second point. My third point: After that Drago Josipovic could appeal for the Defence of alibi, only then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Are there other counsel wishing to address the same issue of alibi? I see none, so I will turn to the Prosecutor and ask him whether they may assist us in this particular point, either right away or in due course.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Well, if you wish me to state a few points on this matter, I shall do so. And there after I could complement my oral observation with written arguments submitted at a later stage. I somehow share this difficulty expressed by the Defence counsel to a certain extent. The Rule, Rule 67, on the communication of evidence on reciprocal disclosure and the steps to be complied with in the case of defence of alibi, all of this is perfectly clear. The text is unambiguous. It remains to be seen as of what moment, as of what state we find ourselves in a situation of alibi. Is it from the point onwards when somebody alleges not to have been present at the scene of a specific crime the accused is charge with? Or does it happen only then when an accused maintains that on the day of the events, in this instance on the 16th of April, the accused was not present in the immediate area? This is to be appreciated in the last instance by you, Your Honours. But my view is as follows: In this case most of the accused, five out of six of them, are accused of, as crimes against humanity, of taking part in the attack launched against the civilian population, the Muslim civilian population in Ahmici on the 16th of April of 1993, and also they are charged with having committed in the context of such an attack, having committed a number of specific criminal offences. Therefore, means of defence based on alibi can only be summarised by the accused as the allegation that they were not present on the 16th of April at the scene of the crimes. However, if they maintain that they were in another city, in another town, in another country, they should be in a position to provide to the judges, and also at the hearing, to provide evidence that can be examined and cross-examined. We then find ourselves within the terms of Rule 67(A) second i. If the Defence aims at establishing before this Tribunal that the accused were well in Ahmici but were not at scenes of the crimes then committed, for instance, were not in the house or on the premises of the house of Sejad Ahmic. Then I do not believe we are in a case of alibi, we are in a means of defence as to the merits. And then the Defence would claim that the accused did not commit the crimes with which they are charged. Then maybe they will try and introduce evidence to that effect. But my personal view, and I certainly defer to the determinations made by the Tribunal, I believe that in such a context, we are not dealing with a defence of alibi, strict assensu. Given the circumstances, it would mean, then, that one or several of the accused were not in Ahmici at the time when the crime of persecution, which characterised the 16th of April, 1993 attack were committed. But I defer to the higher judgement of this Tribunal. It is a very difficult, tough legal issue, indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: We agree with your interpretation of the alibi, defence of alibi, namely that it should only apply or should be relied upon when it is claimed that an accused was not in Ahmici on that particular day, 16th of April, or not in the country. But this defence of alibi cannot apply to somebody when it is claimed that he was there but not doing what he is accused of having done. So therefore, your interpretation is regarded by the Trial Chamber as the proper and sound one. As for the question raised by counsel for Josipovic, by Mr. Susak, and this is relating particularly to the accused Josipovic; probably you may wish to address the points addressed by Mr. Susak in your opening statement, if you are in a position to do so, so as to see whether or not you may to clarify your position with regard to the crimes alleged to be committed by Mr. Josipovic. Do you think you could do so when you are moving on to your opening statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: I shall endeavour to do so, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. All right. I think we could now move on to a different question, namely, the question we raised this morning and on which Mr. Krajina was asked to dwell. I wonder whether Mr. Krajina could elaborate upon the various reasons set out in the motion for Vlatko Kupreskic. You may remember that this morning I drew the attention of Defence counsel in particular to some paragraphs of that motion, and these are the paragraphs, 19 through 24. Why? Because I feel, my personal feeling, but I hope the Court may get some clarification on these items, is that probably some of the queries made in those paragraphs and some of the criticisms levelled by the Defence counsel against the Prosecutor, probably they arrive out of some sort of misunderstanding about the proper role of the Prosecution and the possibility for Defence counsel to cross-examine witnesses, Prosecution witnesses. But still, as I say, to clarify the matter, probably it's better for Mr. Krajina to restate their position on this item, his particular position, and the position of Defence counsel for Vlatko Kupreskic so we may ask, then, the Prosecutor to respond and come to some sort of conclusion on this particular matter. Mr. Krajina could you be so kind as to address this issue?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: Mr. President, thank you. Before addressing this particular matter, I should like to make a request. It has to do with the previous ruling about my request for a co-counsel, assignment of co-counsel. Something is not quite clear to us. We fear that this decision taken this morning was based on a previous request that we made in June of this year. However, on the 11th of August, this year, we submitted a new request to the Trial Chamber asking its approval for the co-defence, co-counsel status for our colleague, Mr. Par, in closing evidence showing that he qualifies for this post. I don't know whether the Trial Chamber had this request at its disposal, but on the 3rd of August we received a written answer from the Registry which was favourable to our request; however, it was noted that the final decision, of course, rests with the Trial Chamber. Therefore, if the Trial Chamber was not familiar with this most recent request, together with its enclosure, and we gave a copy during the break to the Registrar requesting she forward it to the members of the Trial Chamber, so I hope you have now received it. If you consider that I should continue, I will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: Regarding the clarifications requested, regarding paragraphs 19 through 24 of our motion for a separate hearing, I shall try to briefly present our position. The motion for the withdrawal of the indictment was based on our conviction that the Prosecution witnesses will not come to trial to confirm the allegations from the indictment, because their statements made in 1993, 1994 and 1995, in our view, are not relevant; as they were made before local police bodies and local investigators. The Prosecutor interpreted this position of ours in such a way by expressing concern that we were infringing upon the Trial Chamber's decision of the 16th of June, prohibiting contact with witnesses. In paragraphs from 19 to 24, we express our concern that the Prosecutor is applying tactics with the witnesses by naming certain people as witnesses, even though the Prosecution knows that they will not appear in court. The Prosecution is still keeping those witnesses under protection whereby it is impossible for the Defence to have access to them. In today's argument of the Prosecution, he has also said that he will not give the statements of witnesses that he knows will not appear. That is why we asked for a separate hearing, prior to trial, to examine the allegations made by the Prosecution regarding the Defence's contacts with the witness, also to indicate the pressure to which witnesses are exposed by the local police, and that is why we made such a request and why I am repeating that request on this occasion, that you allow me to highlight a few more points linked to this problem. In connection with the concern expressed by the Prosecutor on the possible violation of a ruling by the Trial Chamber regarding contacts with witnesses after the 16th of June, the Defence counsel of Vlatko Kupreskic has submitted to the Trial Chamber all clarifications and statements. We are also ready, at the request of the Trial Chamber, to provide additional explanations and to answer any questions that would contribute to further clarification of these points, for the simple reason that we have no cause to conceal anything in these proceedings. It is the position of the Defence that no one from the Defence or people connected with the Defence of Vlatko Kupreskic had any contact with Prosecution witnesses after the decision of the Trial Chamber of the 16th of June, 1998. The Prosecutor has not offered any evidence that would contest this, and the concern, the alleged concern of the Prosecutor, is, in our view, a tactical move designed to present Vlatko Kupreskic's defence in a negative light. The contact that we had before the 16th of June, that is, contact made with the witnesses by the wife of the accused and other persons who contacted the witnesses and who were later identified by the Prosecution as Prosecution witnesses, we feel that those contacts were quite in order. At that time, there was no prohibition on contact, nor was any kind of pressure exerted on those witnesses, nor were any financial offers made to them. Of course, the Prosecutor claims the opposite, as can be seen from his submissions. The statements offered in support of these allegations, there are hints of some kind of financial offers made. But the Prosecutor has forgotten to mention that the witnesses that he refers to did not go to the police to complain about this but, on the contrary, the police came to pick them up when they learnt that they had had contact with people linked to the accused Vlatko Kupreskic. The Trial Chamber, in our view, will find it easy to establish the real truth regarding the allegations about impermissible contact with witnesses, for all of these witnesses will probably be called and interviewed in this courtroom and we will be able to hear from them directly what the real truth is and what was the nature of the contacts that anybody had with them. A second and, in our view, equally important point in this area and which prompted us to ask for a separate hearing, has to do with the influence on witnesses exerted by the police responsible for supervising them. I shall try briefly to explain our position in this connection. From the moment the indictment was confirmed, my learned colleague, the Prosecutor, informally divided all witnesses into Muslims and Croats, considering the Muslim witnesses as Prosecution witnesses. At our last Status Conference on the 15th of May this year, after the Prosecutor's statement, we opposed this thesis, considering it to be unacceptable. Muslim witnesses have been placed under police supervision, probably upon instructions from the Office of the Prosecutor. Any contact by the Defence with these witnesses has thereby been prevented, even before the decision of the Trial Chamber of the 16th of June, because those witnesses, Muslims, if they were to have contact with people linked to the accused, would immediately be called in by the police for questioning, and the persons with them, or those that may have contacted them, are even arrested and questioned by the police and even physically harassed. We have evidence to corroborate all this. We have submitted to the Trial Chamber and the Prosecutor the documents in support of our request. These witnesses fear the police in the environment in which they live if they were to make statements that could be in support of the defence of the accused. I think it is common knowledge that the interest of the police who supervise these people is, for all the accused Croats, to be condemned, regardless of whether there is evidence of their responsibility or not. In the name of the defence of the accused Vlatko Kupreskic and on the basis of our experience so far in working on this case, we wish to draw the attention of the Trial Chamber to the existence of impermissible interference with the witnesses on the part of local bodies supervising the witnesses. They prevent them from making statements that would be in support of the Defence and, at the same time, they pressure them to support the indictment at all cost. This can be seen from the statements given to us by the Prosecutor in which the same witnesses, who were questioned on a number of occasions by various local bodies, give biased and differing reports on the same events. That is why we appeal to the Trial Chamber, in the course of the presentation of evidence and the examination of witnesses, to devote equal attention to this objection of ours as well as the objections made by the Prosecution about alleged interference with witnesses. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. I wonder whether the Prosecutor could comment on these points?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Very briefly, Mr. President. I fail to understand what the purpose is of the motion submitted to the Court. I believe I understood, but this may be wrong. I understood that this request, this motion, was for a severance of instances of trials, also that the indictment would be withdrawn, but this is not very logical because that would mean that we would try Mr. Vlatko Kupreskic before the trial has actually begun. I would like to state two things in this respect: We know -- and last May your Tribunal, your Chamber, devoted some time to this issue -- we know that there were illegal contacts made between the Defence counsel and specific witnesses. Money was offered. This is certainly inadmissible in this trial as it is inadmissible in all trials. This situation was duly taken into account by your Chamber, which did not rule out any contact between Bosnian witnesses and the Defence; however, you said that specific measures had to be taken to ensure protection, which is quite normal. The procedure you wanted to set up for such contacts never really was operational. However, this never meant that the Defence counsel were precluded from having contact with specific witnesses on account of their nationality or of their ethnic background. This has never been the view of the Prosecution and this was not enshrined in the Court order. We were somewhat surprised and worried at reading in one of the motions filed by the Defence of Vlatko Kupreskic that there was this bold statement according to which Prosecution witnesses will not come to testify in this court on the basis of what happened, and we wondered whether violation of the order issued by the Tribunal had not been committed, but I have to date no clues as to the occurrence of such a violation. I have no evidence of any violation of the Court order of the 20th of May by the Defence counsel. However, I do state that given the very sensitive nature of this issue, if a witness, a Prosecution witness, allegedly approached by the Defence, would not accept to testify, he would not communicate to us the reasons for his refusal to testify. We have not been instructed of any illegal contacts by Defence counsel, but I do want to reserve the right to mention any such future occurrence, should they happen, in which case I would turn to the Tribunal to pass on such evidence. But I have no clues to the effect to date, and I hope that the matter can be settled for the time being by these very remarks. Thank you very much, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Let me try to sum up at least the main points because so many points have been made. As for the question of a separate trial, I think this matter has already been dealt with by Judge Mumba in the order we mentioned before, which is, of course, the 11th of August, 1998, and, of course, that means that we will not hold separate hearings for Vlatko Kupreskic; and as for the credibility of the evidence, this is, of course, a matter which relates to the merits of the trial and will be dealt with in due course. As for the statement or the claim by Mr. Krajina whereby some witness statements are not relevant because they were made before police investigators, again is a matter which may be looked into in due course. For the time being, we don't need to pronounce on this matter. The third point is about the so-called impermissible contacts with witnesses, and the Prosecutor has just stated that they are not claiming that after a particular date, the date which was set by the Trial Chamber, any such contacts have been made by the Defence counsel, family, relatives, and so on, with witnesses. Of course, the Defence counsel are free to get in touch with the Prosecution witnesses, however, after complying with the conditions set out in the order issued by this Trial Chamber; namely, they should go through the Prosecutor or inform the Prosecutor that such contacts are being made. A fourth point has been made by Mr. Krajina, who has repeatedly spoken of tactics or tactical moves by the Prosecutor, and they would consist of the Prosecutor naming witnesses that they would then not call to testify before the Trial Chamber. I am at a loss to understand the significance of this claim because if the Defence counsel feel that those witnesses may be important for the Defence, they may, of course, contact those witnesses, those Prosecution witnesses, always after complying with the conditions I just referred to, and afterwards, they may decide, if those witnesses are not called by the Prosecution, that they themselves, the Defence, will call them as Defence witnesses. If witnesses are called, they, of course, may be cross-examined by the Defence counsel. So therefore, I think that, as I expected, the airing of the various criticisms and claims and the discussion here in court has contributed to clarifying that there is no major issue to be dealt with at this juncture here in court. Let me, therefore, quickly turn to the question of the appointment of Mr. Par as co-counsel. We were actually handed a document at lunch time, a document which has been filed on the 17th of August, namely today, a document reproducing the request submitted by Mr. Krajina for the assignment of co-counsel and a letter sent to him by the Registrar, and, actually, it is true what Mr. Krajina said, that in her letter the Registrar wrote to Mr. Krajina that this was a matter on which the Registrar wished the Trial Chamber to pass our judgement on, and so therefore, she left this matter for us to decide. However, I would stick to what we said this morning, to our ruling, because, as I said before, we are very keen to be consistent with the judicial practice of this Tribunal, the various Trial Chambers, and also stick to the precedents set by our own Trial Chamber and other Trial Chambers. For the time being, it is apparent from what members of the registry told us yesterday, on Sunday, namely that Article 14 of the directive, the directive on assignment of Defence counsel of 10th July, 1998, the requirements laid down in this Article 14 are not met in this particular case, and on the basis of this assessment and taking into account, as I say, the precedents of our Tribunal, we confirm our ruling that Mr. Par is granted the status of legal assistant but not of co-counsel. I propose now that since we have, I think, dealt with all matters which we raised this morning or were raised this morning by the Prosecutor and the Defence, I propose that I quickly move on to a few housekeeping matters. These are a few practical questions. First of all, we insist that the parties should fully comply with the guidelines we set out and circulated a few months ago, the guidelines for the trial which have been also handed in writing to Defence counsel. In addition, this is number 2, I would like to draw the attention of all Defence counsel to the new amended provisions of our Rules of Procedure and Evidence which have been reproduced in a booklet. I hope that you all have received a copy of this booklet. You will have noticed that quite a few Rules of Procedure and Evidence have been amended, revised, by the Plenary Session of the Tribunal, some other provisions have been added, and please take into account that we shall apply all those provisions, new provisions, amended provisions, as long as they do not affect or compress the rights of the Defence. That is a matter which we discussed this morning. This applies in particular to a new provision on the limits of cross-examination. You may have noticed that there is a new rule on cross-examination, there are new rules on the pre-trial Judge, pre-trial Conference, and also a pre-trial Defence Conference. Actually, we hope that we will be in a position to hold such a conference towards the end of the Prosecution case or, if Defence counsel prefer, at the end of the Prosecution case we will hold this particular conference so as to better organise the Defence case, the practicalities of the Defence case. Again, third point, practical matters, we intend to, as for the sitting hours, we start every morning at 9.30, have a break at 11.00, resume at 11.30, and stop at 12.30. In the afternoon, again we will have a break of half an hour. We will reconvene at 2.00 and finish at 5.00, so from 2.00 to 5.00 with a break from 3.30 to 4.00. Since we have to deal also with other matters concerning other trials, we will need at least half a day off, and we suggest that Friday afternoon should be off. On Friday, if you agree, we would like to sit until 1.00 and then have the Friday afternoon off so that we could attend to other matters. As from now, I should say that there will be probably one day off, the 31st of August afternoon, the afternoon. We will not hold any hearing on that afternoon, the 31st of August. I think it is a Monday. It is a Monday. I move on to my fourth point. These are really down-to-earth practicalities. To save as much time as possible, we would like to suggest that each morning, after the registrar has called the case, we will dispense with the appearances. If there is any change in the appearances, you will let us know or you will tell the registrar so we will not even waste our time in calling for the appearances; and when we come to the production of evidence, in particular, witnesses, we would like to start from the assumption that documents tendered into evidence by one party will be admitted into evidence if not objected to by the other party. So that I don't need each time to ask the other party, "Do you object to the admission into evidence of this particular exhibit?" If, therefore, no objection is made after the proffer of one party to give in evidence the particular exhibit, it is assumed that that document is admitted into evidence. A very practical measure again to save time. We will think of other measures designed to speed up our proceedings. We have a few other points, but some of them have already been covered, and so therefore, if you don't have any other matter, I think we could now turn to the Prosecutor and ask whether they are prepared to make their opening statement. However, before doing so, let me very quickly go through the list of witnesses just for one minute because this may be a point to be raised before the opening statement of the Prosecutor. I noticed -- I have so many lists that now I can't find it -- but I noticed that there are 32, I counted 32 Prosecution witnesses who, according to the Prosecutor, will only address Count 1. I wonder whether the Prosecutor -- this is just a query -- whether the Prosecutor needs so many witnesses only for Count 1, and I assume, having read some, not all of them, some of the witness statements, relevant witness statements, that those witnesses are not going to testify on any particular accused. They will not deal with the question of whether or not the accused were there or committed the alleged crimes, they will only address the question of persecution and so on. If this is so -- but I may be wrong, and I stand to be corrected -- then again we, the Court, wonder whether you really need so many witnesses. But, as I say, you don't need to respond now. You may need to ponder this matter and, in due course, decide whether or not to drop some of those particular witnesses because we could then shorten the list of witnesses. As I say, since we don't need a response from you right away, we may ask you to make your opening statement if you think that you could finish by 3.30. If not, if you wish to have now a break, we could now rise and start with your opening statement after the break. It is for you to suggest the better course of action.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I can't tell you exactly. I'm not sure that I will be able to complete the opening statement before 3.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: How much time do you need?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Three-quarters of an hour to one hour. I would like to turn to the map, have some comments, and also introduce two video clips.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: But it might be better to adjourn the hearing now and return within -- yes, I think we need 30 minutes every time, as we were told by the registrar, we need 30-minute breaks. So we can adjourn. We shall return at 3.25 sharp, and we shall start with the opening statement. That's fine. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Mr. President, shall I go to the pulpit, or what should I do?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: As you like.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: If you don't mind, I'll stay here. Your Honours, this morning already, and until now we have had discussions that will make it possible for me to shorten my submissions. Your Trial Chamber, as well as the Defence counsel, have received the pre-trial brief which gives you an overview of the Prosecution's intentions for this trial. Through this opening statement I wish to convey to the Court some factual elements, some topographical elements, and that such elements will be useful to the Court as soon as we hear the first Prosecution witnesses. And they will be useful, too, when it comes to the Defence case. These topographical and factual elements will be challenged by the Defence at some stage, I'm sure. Although, it might not be necessary to come back to them during the proceedings. To start with, I shall describe in broad terms what happened exactly and precisely on the 16th of April in Ahmici. What took place was an ethnic cleansing operation directed by a military unit against a civilian population. I shall be brief, but I think it is necessary to set up the frame, the context in which the Prosecution witnesses will be better understood in the days to come. And then equally briefly, for indeed all these points were stated in the pre-trial brief, I shall make some observations as to the legal characterisation against the excused, but let's speak about the location. I think it is necessary for an investigator, for a judge to know the places we're going to be faced with at the beginning of a trial. Let me get closer to the map, and I'll take, I'll use the microphone located close to the map. This photograph, this aerial photograph shows you the Lasva River Valley. We are some 90 kilometres north-west of Sarajevo. The Lasva River Valley is named after a river which you see meandering here, and which goes further towards the south-west of the area. The major town of Zenica is mainly inhabited by Muslims and lies in this direction which I'm showing, some 15 kilometres away and can be reached easily either through this road extending into the Lasva River Valley, or through this mountain road that goes uphill, goes through the top of the mountain to get to Zenica. There were two areas which were mainly inhabited by Croats in this valley. There is Busovaca, which you can see here towards the top, and also the town of Vitez, which you see here. However, there is a major neighbourhood inhabited, or used to be inhabited by Muslims in Vitez. The neighbourhood no longer exists today, it was destroyed in the early hours of the 16th of April, 1993, as was Ahmici was destroyed, too. Ahmici is located in these lines that have been drawn into a rectangle. I draw your attention to two sides, this one on the road between Busovaca and Vitez going further towards Travnik. This was known as the Bungalow, a former hotel, a former restaurant. Then, and when I mean then, I mean in early 1993, was inhabited by a Croat unit, the unit of the Jokeri or Jokers. We shall have the opportunity to come back to the various actions carried out by the Jokeri. The second site is located here. The Dubravica school. This is a relevant site, because a large number of the Muslim inhabitants who used to live in Ahmici, that's where they were rounded up and detained for some 14 days, up until the time when the Red Cross intervened and secured their release. This is the Dubravica school. And then towards late '92 and early '93, you have the front line against the Serbs in this direction towards the north-west, some 30 kilometres away from Vitez, beyond the cities of Travnik and Turbe. And we apologise for this, the northern direction is more towards what is usually described as the south, but if we had used the proper cardinal points we would not have been able to show you the whole area to be investigated. And then I'm going to show you the part that has been blown up, to show you the actual village of Ahmici. I may ask the help of the usher for the map to be produced. Can you see this map or photograph? This aerial photograph has the north, actually it's towards the west, and this is an enlarged section of this first photograph I just showed you. You find the road, this is a regional road along the valley from Busovaca to Vitez, you can see the Bungalow here, and towards the centre of the photograph you have most of the houses making up the village of Ahmici. However, as the inhabitants themselves put it, whether they are Croats or Muslims, there are also various names given, traditional names given to the various parts of the village. For instance, this is an area called the Donji Ahmici, or the lower Ahmici. And as you go up the hill you come across an area sometimes called Sutra (Phoen). You go further along the road that leads to the forest and you come across an area often called Grabovi. Still further towards the top, then you come to upper Ahmici or Gornji Ahmici. And this area shown here people tend to call it Zume, close to Santici. And this last one I have shown you is Pirici. Areas inhabited by Croats and Muslims in 1993 are delineated and separated. You can take this as a landmark, a cemetery, this is used by many witnesses as a landmark, because you can't miss it. It is very visible from everywhere. There is another landmark that of the Pican cafe, a Croat place close to the main road, and it will be a major landmark for many witnesses. The area of Zume Santici was predominantly an area inhabited by Croats. There is another Croat area around Sutra Grabovi with, in particular, what will be termed by many witnesses the Kupreskic houses, in other words, many members of the Kupreskic family owned a house in that area. Vlatko Kupreskic, one of the accused, has his house here, and his shop was here. The accused Mirjan Kupreskic owned a house here. Zoran's house was here. Dragon Papic owned a house here on the other side of the road and Mr. Josipovic owned a house here, further down. As to Mr. Santic, he does not live in this area. He lives towards the town of Vitez, which can be reached along this road only four kilometres away. So, this is what I wanted to show you by way of these photographs. If you do not mind, we shall carry on this topographical discovery with a video clip. This was shot in 1993, following the events -- '96, sorry. A long time after the events, but showing the village of Ahmici in the condition it was between 1993 and today. There is practically no difference whatsoever between the village then and the village now. With one exception, some of the former inhabitants, Muslim inhabitants of Ahmici where -- the census of NGOs of various governments -- have started clearing the rubble and the ruins and have started building their houses again. None of the houses formerly inhabited by Muslims is today inhabited by Muslims, but there are a few attempts at rebuilding. Such attempts have been started on some of the hills and especially, they all take place in Gornji Ahmici, in upper Ahmici, where they were exclusively Muslim inhabited houses prior to 1993. While viewing the video clip we are going to see three various phases. The first phase was shot from a helicopter and we shall see the lower Mosque, we shall carry on to the upper Mosque and then we shall make a loop and come back to the initial point. The second sequence taken by car will start from this forking off of the main road to its secondary road, we'll go up to the centre of Ahmici, Sutra Grabovi and we'll take this small road to see the Kupreskic houses and we shall return to the larger path to go back or go up to upper Ahmici. We have a short section of the road, the main road we will be able to see the front houses of the Zume neighbourhood, we will see the Pican cafe. We shall catch glimpse of a house that used to be located in this Croat neighbourhood and which was used at the time of the events in April of 1993 to round up some of the Muslims captured by the HVO forces before the people captured were taken to the Dubrivica school, which I mentioned a few moments ago. If you don't mind I will return to my desk and provide with you some comments as we view the video clip.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: The helicopter is moving towards the north-west along the regional main road. You can see in the centre of the image the catholic cemetery. Now, central in the image is that little road that enables you to reach upper Ahmici. You can see the lower Mosque which used to have a minaret, the minaret was blown up by explosive in the evening of the 16th of April, 1993, around the Mosque you can see houses which, by all accounts, are destroyed and unoccupied. Now, towards the lower part of the image you can see the house of Vlatko Kupreskic and the part goes up towards upper Ahmici, and if a few moments you're going to see the upper Mosque which was also extensively destroyed. You can sit here in the middle of the picture and the houses surrounding the Mosque were inhabited by Muslims and the houses were burned or destroyed to the ground. I suppose we're going to see the second part, where we start from the regional road to go up towards upper Ahmici. Stop the image, please. I think you must be informed of this: There is a traditional way of building houses in the area, Croat houses would be of the Swiss chalet types, so two sided roofs, whilst Muslim houses usually had a hipped roof with four sides. That's the rule. But you will notice, especially here on this picture, that there were also many exceptions to this rule, and that some Muslim houses also had two-sided roofs, thereby showing no distinctive sign to somebody not being from the village. There was no difference between that house and a Croat house. We will mention the house of Mesic Pjanic (Phoen) in the course of this week. All of the houses along the road have two-sided roofs, so nothing would differentiate a Muslim house from a Croat house along that road. We can carry on, yes, please go on. You can see here a Muslim house with this four-sided roof. You can only see the roof structure because there is no roofing material anymore, and here you have the Mosque. What you see here is the school or what used to be the school, it was also destroyed on the 16th of April, 1993. However, here you can see intact Croat houses. To the right you can see a shop owned by Vlatko Kupreskic, his house was close by to the right of the shop. And straight behind, tens of metres away, there is the house of Saki Pafmic (Phoen), or rather the ruins of what remains of the house, and we will mention this during this week of proceedings. We're moving now towards the Kupreskic houses. Towards the right, yes, carry on, this house is not the house of one of the accused; however, on the other side you've got the houses of Zoran and Mirjan Kupreskic. Here's Mirjan Kupreskic's house, while Zoran's house is straight in front of this one. Vlatko Kupreskic's house is straight on the left. We fork off and go through this little path to upper Ahmici, back in 1993 this area was exclusively inhabited by Muslims, and all the houses still today are destroyed. In front of us now to the right is the upper Mosque. Here it is. As you can see, very extensively destroyed. We are now in upper Ahmici where all the houses were destroyed on the 16th of April, '93. Some of which are now being rebuilt or have work done to it, for instance, to rebuild the roof frames. Now, we have reached the upper part, the highest point in Ahmici. The third clip was made on the regional road in the direction of Vitez, and we will see, to the right of that road, the houses of Zume, houses which were virtually all Croat, and the Pican cafe at the end of this clip.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Can you stop that? The houses that we see, all of them with two slopes, they're all Croat houses, houses at the end of the Zume area, the Pican cafe is on the right-hand side of the screen, and it was here that a certain number of detainees were rounded up, and we will see this spot on the left-hand side of the screen. Mr. President, Your Honours, these were the principal topographical indications that I wanted to present to you, and I think that this film, this video that you have just seen, shows us or illustrates one of the elements of the facts that we need to prove to the court, that is, that on the 16th of April, 180 houses in Ahmici were destroyed, that all the destroyed houses were Muslims', and that almost all the Muslim houses of Ahmici were destroyed. On the other hand, Croat houses remained intact. Not a single one of them was damaged in any significant manner. This is a fact which could have been admitted by the Defence in its pre-trial brief. Also, the Defence could have admitted the census data from 1991 according to which, in 1993, at the beginning of 1993 or at the end of 1992, Ahmici had 466 inhabitants of whom 356 were Muslim and 87 Croat, which means a very large majority were Muslims. Also something else that the Defence cannot contest, that at the end of 1992 and the beginning of 1993, there was a certain number of Muslim refugees staying in Ahmici which were chased out of their homes by the fighting on the front against the Serbs and which came to live with their families in Ahmici. Very often, these people came in 1992, at the end of the summer, and sometimes even at the beginning of 1993. These refugees, all Muslims, were not well-known among the local population, so that it is difficult to assess exactly the number, but we can say that about 50 refugees, who were chased from their homes from the front-line with the Serbs, stayed mostly in weekend houses because in Ahmici, in the lower area, there were a number of smaller houses used before the war by people residing in the cities, and these houses were placed at the disposal, quite naturally, of these refugees. If we compare the village of Ahmici before the 16th of April, '93, and the village of Ahmici in the days that followed and even to this day, we will see that what used to be a Muslim, majority Muslim village, we see hundreds of -- Croat village, and we will also see that this total destruction of Ahmici took place in a very short period of time, a period of time that began on the 16th of April at dawn and which continued in the hours that followed, that is, the next morning, the morning of the 17th. I was struck by the fact that on the wall of the lower mosque, we found the words "48 hours of ashes," and it is rather strange that numerous Muslim villagers said that "48 hours of ashes" was the code name given by the HVO forces to this ethnic cleansing campaign. I will say straight-away that we were not able to prove this assertion which is based basically on a rumour, a persistent rumour, but still a rumour. However, it has been possible to note the total correspondence between this designation of 48 hours of ashes, perhaps it will be better to say of blood and ashes, fully illustrates the pain and suffering of the victims of those events. I will not refer to the political situation in Central Bosnia-Herzegovina at the beginning of 1993. I think that the Tribunal is perfectly familiar with that situation, as it is with the military situation that was prevalent at that point in time, and the existence of an armed conflict opposing the Croats, the Croat authorities of Bosnia, against the authorities of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The army of the Bosnian Croats, the HVO, was present in full strength in the area of Vitez and Busovaca. On the other hand, the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina was virtually absent from this region. The fighting could entail these two armies in Travnik, that is, about 20 kilometres to the west of Vitez, in the region of Ahmici itself and in Ahmici, there were what was known as the Territorial Defence forces, and this Territorial Defence cannot be considered as an armed force. It is a grouping of citizens, based on the voluntary principle, who got together to protect the security of their homes and their families. If they were armed, they were lightly armed. They didn't, each one of them, have a weapon, in principle, and if there was any command structure, there was no real centralised chain of command that would correspond to a military structure. In that period, I am talking about the end of '92, the beginning of 1993, UNPROFOR was present in the area. Vitez, Ahmici belonged to the area of responsibility of the British battalion that was based in Vitez and whose commander at the time was Colonel Stewart and his assistant was Colonel Watters, who will be our first witness and who will speak, if the Court allows it, after me. The mission of UNPROFOR was to protect humanitarian convoys, to protect the population, of course, fully respecting the principle of impartiality regarding the conflict in which various communities were opposed against one another in Central Bosnia as in the rest of Bosnia-Herzegovina. But this British battalion area, or the members of the battalion, were present and their testimony is important for an understanding of the situation, and they were observers which your Tribunal, I am sure, will listen to with great attention. Regarding the forces present in Busovaca and Vitez, they will have important information to convey to you. At the end of 1992 and the beginning of 1993, we find ourselves in a situation of an armed conflict between the Bosnian authorities and the Bosnian Croat authorities, the alliance that united them against a common enemy, the Serbs, having completely been broken in the meantime. In this situation of an armed conflict, it had very direct impact on the situation in Ahmici. In October 1992, in Ahmici, an event occurred which was an immediate reflection of the armed conflict which had swept to Central Bosnia at the time. In the second half of October 1992, combat broke out in Travnik between elements of the Bosnian army and elements or units of the HVO. The Territorial Defence of Ahmici placed on the road linking Busovaca and Vitez and then on to Travnik a roadblock which, in the view of their authors, was to prevent HVO forces from Busovaca to make progress towards Travnik and thus to reinforce the forces engaged in the conflict in the region of Travnik. This roadblock on the road at Ahmici was erected on the 19th of October. It was manned by some 30 Muslims from the village of Ahmici and, as we will show in the course of our case, the 30 or so men were insufficiently armed for the task they assigned themselves and they had very little command. This provoked the fury of the HVO which immediately demanded the deblocking of the road and which, after some threats at dawn on the 20th of October, launched a resolute attack because the HVO used heavy weapons against the roadblock, against the barricade but, it is also important to note, also against non-military targets, that is, houses or some houses which were in the lower part of Ahmici. At the beginning of the afternoon, members of the Territorial Defence of Ahmici found themselves in a weaker position; they withdrew and opened the way to the HVO. More than 20 houses were destroyed, the minaret of the lower mosque was seriously damaged, and this target was obviously intentionally targeted, and it cannot, under any circumstances, be considered a military target. A young man of 15, Alija Pezer, a non-combatant, was killed by a sniper during that day. After that event of the 20th of October, 1992, the situation in Ahmici between the communities became extremely tense. The violence throughout that period, from October '92 until April 1993, was rampant and, from time to time, it would explode. The HVO forces, in fact, in Ahmici, as in Vitez, required total subordination of the Muslims. They required the surrender of weapons. They demanded the right to be able to control any movement by the Muslims. They demanded a curfew to be applied to the Muslims but not to the Croats. At the beginning of 1993, a unit that called themselves the Jokers established itself in the Bungalow, and members of this unit, during the weeks that followed until April 1993, will distinguish themselves in particular by their brutality towards the civilian population and their provocation consisting, among other things, of firing at roads, firing at cars or buildings along the road, and very many Muslims in that period were victimised by these acts of provocation which were elements of persecution. A few weeks before the tragedy in April, a person called Esad Salkic, who lived in Nadioci, which is very close to Ahmici, in the direction of the Bungalow, was killed in his house because he refused to surrender a weapon demanded by the HVO. At that point in time, the Muslims decided to protect themselves with night guards. The Croats reacted immediately, demanding that these patrols be abolished, and in the discussions that ensued between the Muslims and Croats of Ahmici, upon a suggestion, made a conciliatory suggestion by the Muslims that there should be joint patrols by the Croats and the Muslims, the Croat representatives, among whom Zoran Kupreskic, invoked superior orders and said that there was no question of ensuring security of the civilian population with joint patrols. On the 15th of April, during a meeting, the Muslims were given assurances that no steps would be taken against them and that their safety was fully ensured in the region. Even though tension was running high between the two communities and even though difficulties were considerable and even though the impact of the armed conflict was significant in Ahmici, the majority of the witnesses will tell you, and not one of them will tell you that not one of them could have imagined that the events of the 16th of April could take place. When we listen to the various witnesses speaking about that day, this attack was against a civilian population, the attack of 16th of April, which reflected a determination and a savagery that was quite unique. That attack did not have any aspect of an improvisation. It was an episode of an HVO offensive against Muslim settlements throughout the Lasva River Valley, and particularly in Vitez and Ahmici, certainly a most conspicuous episode but only an episode of this overall offensive. The attack started about 5.30 in the morning. They were supported with heavy weapons, anti-aircraft guns in particular charged with explosives and with incendiary bullets. The ground forces, the infantry belonging to the HVO and the Jokers unit, which were wearing camouflage uniforms in the case of the HVO and black uniforms in the case of the Jokers, they were armed with automatic rifles, with mortars, with incendiary weapons, and this military force was deployed first in the lower part of Ahmici against an exclusively civilian population, women, children, and elderly, which were awoken from their sleep and were still wearing night-clothes, night-gowns. It should be known that the attack started simultaneously in Grabovi. The village was encircled, shelled from the outside, but also attacked from within from the area of the Kupreskic houses, that is, the locality known as Grabovi. This action continued throughout the day; they went from one house to another. The soldiers were perfectly organised, they knew what they had to do, they communicated by radio. Each one of them carried a ribbon which indicated their task or the zone they were assigned to. They fired at the houses. They ordered the inhabitants to come out. In principal, they separated the men from the women. In most cases, they shot the men on the spot, and they took the women and the children to detention centres. Sometimes women and children were also killed because soldiers fired on several occasions on people who tried to flee, whoever they may have been, whether they were children or adults. In all the cases, the soldiers set fire to the houses. The members of the UNPROFOR, the British battalion of UNPROFOR, as of 11.00 that morning and on several occasions throughout the day, entered Ahmici to assist the wounded, to try to protect the women and the children, to try to evacuate them to a safe area. When the members of the British battalion entered Ahmici with their armoured vehicle, the HVO forces moved away, they didn't stop shooting; but as soon as the British battalion withdrew from Ahmici, the HVO forces came back again and continued their operation. The members of the British battalion did a lot for the civilian population and their testimony is important. They helped many Muslim civilians, many women and children, and I think that in the dramatic circumstances they found themselves in, they did everything that they could within their mandate. Those of them who were there in Ahmici will convey to you the feelings that they had at the time. This continued throughout the day. In the early morning hours of the next day, it was completed. Ahmici could not resist. Only a few Muslims, belonging to the Territorial Defence with some light arms, did fire a couple of shots. There never was a single Croatian victim alleged, so that the resistance of the TO was symbolic. It was the resistance of men trying to protect their families from soldiers threatening their lives. This operation provoked a great deal of emotion, it stupefied many witnesses, eyewitnesses, the scope of the destruction, the number of victims, some of whose bodies were still in the buildings 15 days after the operation, all this was noted by various persons, either members of the UNPROFOR or members belonging to the U.N. or to European or international institutions. I would like to suggest that we now see a very brief video which quite precisely reflects the emotions felt 15 days after the event because some reports were aired about this massacre. This film was made by the BBC News, it was aired by BBC News at the beginning of May 1993 when British soldiers of UNPROFOR came to the village to investigate and to carry out some of the bodies from the rubble. Perhaps we can now look at this video? (Videotape played).

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: There is the second part to it. Needless to say, we shall submit to the Defence a copy of the video clips as well as copies of the aerial photographs that are introduced in the beginning of my opening statement. Let me add this: In Vitez on the 28th of April, 1993, 12 days, that is, after the attack, 99 bodies, some of which beyond recognition, burned beyond recognition, were buried in some mass graves dug by the members of the British battalion. You shall see footage of the burial ceremony. There are four members of the Ahmic family that were later discovered by the BritBat members in the ruins of the torched house, were buried on the 6th of May in the same cemetery. This means there are today 103 bodies, the bodies of the victims of the HVO attack in the Lasva River Valley. However, 45 bodies could not be identified before they were buried, and we know that all of the victims were not from Ahmici. We know that a lot of the victims of Ahmici have not been buried in the Vitez cemetery. And we, but especially the families, do not know where their next of kin were buried. There was a rumour, according to which there was a clandestine cemetery set up by the Croats for unknown reasons. This was never established or confirmed, but it nevertheless remains that a lot of families still don't know today where their parents were buried. During these trial proceedings, we shall endeavour to establish as accurately as we can the number of civilian victims in Ahmici. This figure could be some 110 people of whom over 30 women and close to 20 children or teenagers under 18 years of age. This is a considerable amount of children and teenagers. This will be shown and established with as much accuracy as is possible today. The witnesses you will come to hear, the inhabitants of Ahmici will tell of their personal tragedies, the ones they experienced during those days, but also in the ensuing months and years. Let me insist on the fact that there were individual tragedies in Ahmici that have left no traces, no survivors, no witnesses. I would like to speak of the killing fields, as some witnesses will, too, close to the lower part of Ahmici. This was the name given by the members of the British battalion when they saw what they had to see in the massacre. In the middle of the 16th of April in those killing fields across the Catholic cemetery, the members of the British battalion saw some 20 bodies, bodies of civilian people, some were female bodies, some were the bodies of children, one woman was killed while she was still holding the hand of a child. There is another tragedy, that of this father and his child whom he was holding in his arms, and they were both killed, shot dead on their doorstep. Another tragedy, among many others, is that of Sejad Ahmic, whose house you've just seen. Colonel Stewart mentioned the victims found near that house. But I must state we have very little information as to what really happened, apart from what Colonel Stewart said, and we have no accurate data on the exact circumstances in which all the members of this family were killed. We are well aware of the fact that the tragedy and the crime of Ahmici is still not known in many of its aspects, but we have a few accurate facts that we will show during these proceedings. And I am sure that the Tribunal and the Court will be convinced of the elements we will show. I will stop here when it comes to the actual facts, time is flying; and if you will allow me, I shall be briefer, to move straight away to the following. Why were the crimes committed in Ahmici in 1993? Why were they crimes against humanity? Pursuant to Article 5 of the Statute, and pursuant to the case law established by this Tribunal. If we look at the motives and the purposes sought by the perpetrators of these crimes, there is no doubt whatsoever they did it on ethnic, political, racial and religious grounds. They wanted to cleanse the area, they wanted to root out the entire community. One community wanted to root out the other. The Tribunal knows that the Vance-Owen Plan was made public in January, 1993, a plan according to which they should be Canton province number 10, to be under Croat administration was Ahmici and Vitez, were to be under province number 10. Most of the inhabitants in that province of Canton were in deed Croats, but there were some municipalities, some hamlets or villages that had a Muslim majority, which was the case in Ahmici. The offensive launched by the HVO against the Muslim civilian dwellings and the civilian population in Ahmici in 1993 did not aim at fighting against the positions of an opposing army; it aims at splitting, separating communities by driving out, by destroying houses, by murdering, by removing, by force transfer and deportation. In so doing they aimed at rooting out the Muslim community from the face of this earth. This operation is beyond any reasonable doubt planned and carried out on a systematic, in a systematic fashion at large scale. The forces involved in the Ahmici operation, in the operation against Ahmici, the means used, the material, equipment, the military resources involved implied that everything had been planned and organised at all levels of the military command. Planning and preparation implies orders that have been prepared, issued, confirmed at all levels of this military hierarchy. And in spite of these important resources, they managed to keep an absolute secrecy in relation to the operation in the days prior to the attack. Not a single Muslim was warned of what was about to happen. As I said before, this operation was part of a general offensive in the Lasva River Valley, against all Muslim positions and houses. It lasted several days, did not come up against any resistance until such time when the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina launched a counter attack. For instance, in Vitez similar facts as those in Ahmici were committed on the same day and Stari Vitez, the Muslim neighbourhood, was totally destroyed on that day. BritBat members will tell that they went out in the early hours of the morning on that day and they saw in Vitez the bodies of civilians lying around in the Muslim neighbourhood while in the Croat neighbourhood everything was calm and no damage had been caused. As a result, I think that the evidence will show that all the men taking part in the operations were carrying orders, complied with such orders, and that they in no way had some personal pursuit in mind. Neither did they want to settle any hostility they may have had towards individual single Muslim neighbours. All the Croats taking part in the operation can be held and must be held responsible for it. Evidence will show that the six accused tried here today took part in the offensive, in a direct fashion with weapons in their hands, or else, alternatively, that they aided and abetted in a very active way, and they also provided logistical support to such operations. We shall prove beyond any reasonable doubt that the six accused back in those days were involved in the HVO forces, had sympathy for nationalistic causes, were subjected to Croat and HVO authority, and even that some of them were fanatics, or behaved in a fanatic way. It is obvious that if you were in the HVO forces, if you were dedicated to a nationalistic cause, that means that you could not remain passive once the village in which you lived was prey to, or was going to undergo such an operation. There was the need for local support, according to military doctrine. The military doctrine made it necessary for military forces penetrating into the village be clearly informed of their targets, that the Muslim houses that looked like Croat houses be shown to them, that the Croat houses to be protected be shown to them, as well. It is unthinkable that an operation of such scale be conducted by military forces that would be alien to the area, to the village. Military logic and doctrine make it necessary for Croats residing in Ahmici to be part of those forces which launched the attack against the village. And the community rationale or doctrine also makes it necessary for the Croats living in Ahmici to be associated with the operation. It is unthinkable that the Croat families or Croat interests in Ahmici would be jeopardised, would be imperilled by such an operation. It was therefore necessary, to the extent possible, that the Croat families be evacuated on the eve of the operation, and this is precisely what happened. And the evidence will show that. And this is another indicator of the involvement of the Croats from Ahmici, and more especially from the six accused tried here today. The evidence will also show that five out of the six accused committed specific crimes during that day. We shall adduce evidence through numerous converging and corroborating testimony. We will show that Zoran and Mirjan Kupreskic are responsible for the destruction of the family of Sakib Ahmic, their closest Muslim neighbours; their father, Naser; the wife, Zehrudina, and their two children Elvis and Sejad. Sakib Ahmic was wounded but survived the attack and he will be here to testify. The credibility of this major witness, that is Sakib Ahmic, will be established through other testimony, but also through crime scene investigation carried out in the ruins of the houses of his family. We will show that Vlatko Kupreskic is also responsible for the death of Fata Pezer for the wounding of Dzenana Pezer, that many witnesses will say that they saw him in the peak of the offensive armed with a weapon close to the house. And witnesses will say he fired with that weapon, which leaves no doubt as to his guilt. And we will also show that Vlado Santic and Drago Josipovic are responsible for the death of Musafer Puscul and for the destruction of his house. They seem to be irrefutable witnesses, even though the Defence did not seem to agree with this, this morning; but this will be established through witnesses in front of you, Your Honours. I shall come to an end by mentioning very briefly the order in which witnesses will be called, in order to give you further information on this. We wanted to call witnesses according to some logical order. We first will deal with the circumstances of the attack with Dragan Papic's participation in the planning and the execution of the attack. At a further stage we shall turn to specific crimes relating to the Pezer family, to the Ahmic family and to the Puscul family, and will look into the their own participation in the attack, but also in the acts of Zoran and Mirjan Kupreskic, to start with, and Vlatko, following with Drago Josipovic and finish with Vladimir Santic. We will try to adhere to this logical order of appearance, but I do beg you to apologise for any possible trouble that may, or difficulty that may crop up later and cause this order to be changed. But as much as we can we shall stick to this logical order of appearance. Thank you very much for your attention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Prosecutor. It is a quarter to five, it is probably pointless to have the first witness, after all it will take more than 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: We were going to call Colonel Watters, who was the deputy of Colonel Stewart at the time. Colonel Stewart was the commander of the BritBat in Vitez, and I do fear that his testimony, the examination-in-chief, but especially the cross-examination might take more than 15 minutes. We are faced with a problem, though. Colonel Watters told us, and he is still a member of the British Army, and he must be back in Great Britain at the latest by tomorrow, end of tomorrow morning. I was probably too long in my opening statement, I'm sorry for that; but exceptionally maybe could we extend the hearing by half an hour and we could begin the examination-in-chief and continue tomorrow morning? I fear that we might not have enough time tomorrow morning. We might, if we start today, we might have more time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Well, this will be an exception, but we agree to work until 5.30. So, you may call your first witness. Which are the witnesses you intend to call tomorrow and the day after tomorrow? Could we follow the order that you gave us in your motion of the 3rd of August?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Yes, but with one exception, Mr. President; some witnesses have to go back to Bosnia quite rapidly, so, I was hoping to be able to -- we have Mr. Akhavan, who is a member of the office of the Prosecutor, and we could postpone his testimony to enable the Bosnian witnesses to be heard before him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: The Defence would request, in order to prepare for the cross-examination, to be given at least a minimum of 48 hours to be informed, 48 hours ahead of the arrival of the witness, who the witness will be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes, I think that's quite sensible. Can I ask the Prosecution whether they are prepared to give the advance notice, 48 hours? I think it's quite proper that they should know the list of witnesses the Prosecution is going, are going to call; are you in a position to do so?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: That's fine, in principle, no objection in principle. I do understand the reason why Defence counsel have formulated such a request, which seems to be quite legitimate. But we sometimes are faced with practical problems, and sometimes they are such that we can't really do anything else, and sometimes the advance notice of 48 hours might not be an accurate one. So, if we make this commitment, please do not take offence if we have to change things at the last minute. But in principle there is no objection to this advance notice. Of course, with the proviso that we have a counterpart, the coordinating counsel could then pass on the information to the other Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: That's fine, but this means that this afternoon, tonight you're going to pass on this to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Yes, tonight we shall submit the list of the next witnesses to the Defence, together with the protective measures requested, that's no problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes, I would like, you should provide to the Defence the list of the witnesses you intend to call until Friday, roughly speaking, that would be fine for the Defence to have an idea of what is going to happen over the week.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: That will be done, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Watters. May I ask you to make the solemn declaration?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Colonel Watters.

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Could you start, Colonel, by telling us what you do for a living?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: I'm a Lieutenant Colonel in the British Army and I'm currently commanding the First Battalion of the Cheshire Regiment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Could you briefly give us a summary of your experience in the British military, if you would?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN SHAUN CHARLES WATTERS
utterances.text: I was commissioned into regiment 25 years ago this month from our military academy. And to date I've served in commands in staff posts in my regiment and in the wider British Army.
